chapters.title: Chapter 261: Good Enough
paragraphs: The Audi rolled into Peak University nearly twenty minutes behind the buses.

Stan guided the car through the evening traffic around the athletic complex and brought it to a smooth stop near the cheerleaders’ drop-off area. The engine settled into a quiet idle as the three women began the slightly reluctant process of gathering their things.
No one seemed particularly eager for the ride to end.
Sophie was the slowest to move.
She turned in her seat to face him properly. Her cheer uniform was slightly rumpled after the long day, and her ponytail had loosened into something softer and less carefully arranged.
"So."
Her eyes were bright despite the exhaustion beneath them.
"What’s next?"
"Zack mentioned some kind of team dinner at the dining hall. They’re hosting it for everyone involved with the game."
He glanced at her.
"Did the cheer captain invite you?"
Sophie nodded.
"Bria invited the entire squad about ten minutes after the final buzzer. Every cheerleader is going."
"You too, Maya?"
Maya leaned forward between the front seats.
"Yep. Bria mentioned it."
A grin spread across her face.
"Honestly, after everything that happened tonight, there’s no way I’m missing it."
Stan nodded and looked over his shoulder toward the back seat.
"Fiona?"
The photographer visibly startled.
"O-oh."
She tightened her grip on the camera bag resting against her chest.
"Bria invited all of us too, so... yes."
A nervous smile appeared.
"I should probably get my photos to the paper first, but... yes. I’ll be there."
"Cool."
The simple response carried the easy certainty that he’d expected nothing else.
"Then I’ll see all three of you there."
A small look of satisfaction appeared on Sophie’s face.
The expression was subtle, but not subtle enough to hide the fact that she had quietly been wondering whether Stan might decide to skip the event entirely.
She leaned across the center console and pressed a quick, warm kiss to the corner of his mouth.
"Don’t be late."
"I won’t."
"I’m serious."
Her eyes narrowed slightly.
"I will personally come to your apartment and drag you there by your shirt collar."
Stan smiled.
"I’ll be there, Sophie."
"Good."
Maya rolled her eyes dramatically.

Still mildly annoyed that Sophie had monopolized the passenger seat for the entire trip, she leaned down from behind, gave Stan a quick peck on the neck, and immediately hopped out of the car before Sophie could comment on it.
"My turn."
The door shut behind her.
Sophie stared after her.
"...Brat."
Maya’s victorious laugh floated back through the window.
Fiona, trying and failing to suppress a smile, carefully climbed out after her with her camera bag balanced securely against her side.
Sophie was the last to leave.
One foot on the pavement, one hand resting on the open door, she lingered for a moment.
Then she looked back at him.
Just one more time.
The smile she gave him was smaller now. Softer.
A little more private.
She lifted a hand and waved.
Stan returned the gesture.
Satisfied, Sophie finally closed the door.
He watched as the three women headed toward the cheer squad’s locker room.
Sophie naturally fell into step beside Maya and looped an arm through hers.
Maya pretended to complain while making absolutely no effort to pull away.
Fiona walked half a step behind them, clutching her camera bag and listening to whatever animated conversation the other two had already started.
From a distance, they looked like an unlikely combination.
And yet somehow, with every passing day, they looked more and more like a group that belonged together.
Stan watched them disappear into the evening crowd. Then he shifted the Audi back into gear. The car pulled smoothly away from the curb and merged back onto the campus road.
His apartment awaited.
The apartment was quiet when Stan stepped inside.
He set his bag down by the door, kicked off his sneakers, and headed straight for the bathroom.
The shower was hot and unhurried—the kind that felt less like cleaning up and more like recovery.
It washed away the accumulated sweat of practice, the thirty-five-minute game, and the lingering residue of adrenaline that always seemed to settle beneath the skin after a high-intensity afternoon.
Stan stood beneath the stream longer than he strictly needed to.
The heat loosened the tension in his shoulders. The noise of the game faded. The chants. The crowd. The roar after the dunk.
All of it gradually settled into memory.
By the time he stepped out, the day finally felt finished. He dried off, pulled on a pair of shorts, and walked toward his closet.
Then he paused.
A campus dinner at the dining hall wasn’t, by any honest interpretation, an event that required formal clothing.
At the same time, showing up in the same jersey and sneakers he’d worn all day felt wrong.
Something in between. The kind of casual that suggested effort without looking like effort.
The kind of outfit that fit naturally into a room full of athletes, cheerleaders, students, and coaches.

After a moment’s consideration, he pulled out a dark fitted henley, a pair of dark trousers cut with clean lines through the leg, and well-worn leather sneakers that sat comfortably between athletic and mature.
Simple, clean, and appropriate. He added a steel watch to his wrist. Nothing flashy.
The sort of watch that looked ordinary to most people and expensive only to those who knew what they were looking at.
A final adjustment of the sleeves. A quick check of the collar. Then he stepped in front of the full-length mirror.
For a few seconds, he studied the reflection looking back at him.
The Stan Harrison in the mirror felt very far removed from the young man who had walked into Sophie’s livestream barely two weeks ago with a fistful of carefully saved bills in his pocket.
A lot had happened since then. The changes weren’t dramatic when viewed one day at a time.
But standing there now, they were impossible to ignore. He looked leaner and sharper. More settled within himself.

The henley emphasized the broad shoulders and athletic frame he had built without making a spectacle of them. The dark colors drew attention naturally toward his face rather than the clothes themselves.
More than anything, there was a quiet confidence in the reflection. Not arrogance and definitely not self-consciousness.
Simply the calm presence of someone who no longer felt the need to prove he belonged in a room.
Stan looked at himself for another second. Then he gave a small nod.
’Good enough.’
Turning away from the mirror, he grabbed his keys from the counter.
The team dinner was waiting.

chapters.title: Chapter 262: The Night Is Just Beginning
paragraphs: In the parking garage, Stan passed the Audi without slowing down and continued toward the Huracán.

The matte-black supercar sat low beneath the overhead lights, its sharp angles and aggressive silhouette casting hard shadows across the concrete floor. Even parked and silent, it possessed a presence that demanded attention.
He pressed the key fob. A soft chirp answered him. The lights flashed and the doors unlocked.
Stan slid into the driver’s seat and settled comfortably behind the wheel. For a brief moment, his hand rested on the leather-wrapped steering wheel as the quiet of the garage surrounded him.
The Audi had been the right choice for practice and the game. Practical, comfortable, forgettable.
The kind of car that let the day be about basketball rather than about what he drove.
The Huracán was none of those things. It was not practical. It was not forgettable.
And on the right kind of evening, that was precisely the point.
Tonight felt like one of those evenings. The campus was still buzzing from the upset victory.
The dunk clip was spreading across social media at a ridiculous pace.
Thousands of students had already seen his name, his face, and that moment hanging above the rim.
A dining hall full of teammates, cheerleaders, coaches, and students was waiting for him.
Showing up in the Huracán felt less like showing off and more like matching the energy of the night.
Stan pressed the ignition. The engine came alive instantly.

A deep, controlled growl rolled through the cabin, the sound rich and mechanical without being excessive. It was the voice of a machine built with one purpose in mind: to make people look up when it arrived.
The dashboard illuminated.
The garage echoed briefly with the low rumble. Stan shifted into gear.
The Huracán eased out of its parking space and glided toward the exit ramp.
Moments later, the matte-black supercar emerged into the evening air.
Campus lights reflected across its bodywork as he headed toward the dining hall, the celebration still waiting for him.
The drive across campus was short. It was also, in its own way, incredibly theatrical.
The matte-black Huracán rolled through the evening-lit roads of Peak University like a celebrity making a scheduled appearance.

Heads turned. Students walking between dorms and study halls instinctively glanced toward the sound of the engine. More than a few already had their phones in hand, doomscrolling through clips from the game, and several lifted them almost automatically when the supercar passed.
Then they realized who was driving. The reactions escalated immediately.
"Isn’t that the student tycoon’s Lamborghini?"
"STAN!"
"THAT’S HIM!"
"HUNDRED-YARD JUMPER, BABY!"
"PEAK!
Laughter followed.
A few students actually jogged alongside the sidewalk for several seconds trying to get a better look.
Stan simply raised a hand in acknowledgment without slowing down. The gesture somehow made the crowd even more excited.
By the time he reached the dining hall, several people were already posting fresh photos online.
The building sat at the edge of the central commons, its large glass windows glowing warmly against the darkening evening.
Stan pulled into the visitor parking lot and guided the Huracán into a space near the entrance.
As the engine shut off, he glanced through the windshield and noticed that nearly every student passing by was slowing down to look at the car.
Several had already stopped entirely. Two students were openly taking pictures. One was recording a video.
Stan found himself mildly amused by the predictability of it all.
The Huracán had never been subtle. He stepped out and locked the car.
Immediately, another small cluster of students started whispering. The wide glass doors of the dining hall stood propped open.
Warm light spilled across the pavement. Music drifted faintly from inside. So did laughter.
The celebration was already well underway.
Just inside the entrance stood Zack. The basketball captain had very obviously stationed himself there with one specific mission in mind.
Intercept Stan the moment he arrived.
The second he spotted him through the glass, his grin widened.
"Bro."
"Zack."
"You actually showed up in the Huracán."
"You sound surprised."
"I’m not surprised."
Zack pointed toward the parking lot behind him. "I’m delighted."
He shook his head. "The energy in there is already insane. You pulling up in the matte-black is going to make it apocalyptic."
Stan considered that. "That’s a strong word."
"It’s the correct word." Zack stepped forward, clapped him on the shoulder, and pulled him into a quick half-hug.
When he stepped back, he was still grinning. "I don’t know if I told you this yet, but Zoey recorded everything."
"You mentioned it.
"The dunk clip just crossed eight million views."
Stan blinked. "Eight?"
"Million." Zack held up a finger for emphasis.
"Eight. Million."
A laugh escaped him.
"Zoey is one notification away from ascending into another plane of existence."
Then his expression softened slightly. More genuine.
"Seriously, though."
He gestured toward the packed dining hall.
"Without you, none of this happens."
His voice carried a sincerity that cut through the jokes. "We don’t beat Velaris Crown."
"We don’t bring the cup home."
"We don’t have half the campus celebrating tonight."
For a brief moment, Zack looked every bit the captain who had carried the hopes of the team all season.
Then the grin returned. "So, on behalf of Peak University..."
He spread his arms dramatically.
"Thanks for casually deciding to become an elite basketball player for one afternoon."
Stan shrugged. "You asked."
"I did."
"And somehow that’s still the craziest part."
Laughing, Zack turned toward the interior of the hall and began walking. "Come on."
The noise grew louder with every step.
"The team’s at the back."
"The cheer squad’s here."
"Half the school is here."
He glanced over his shoulder. "And approximately seventy percent of them are waiting to see if you’re actually real."
Stan followed him through the open doors. Into the warmth. Into the noise. Into the celebration.
The team was waiting. The cheer squad was waiting. Sophie was waiting.
And the rest of the night was just beginning.

It was the voice of a machine built with one purpose in mind: to make people look up when it arrived.
The dashboard illuminated.
The garage echoed briefly with the low rumble.
Stan shifted into gear.
The Huracán eased out of its parking space and glided toward the exit ramp.
Moments later, the matte-black supercar emerged into the evening air.
Campus lights reflected across its bodywork as he headed toward the dining hall, the celebration still waiting for him.
The drive across campus was short.
It was also, in its own way, incredibly theatrical.
The matte-black Huracán rolled through the evening-lit roads of Peak University like a celebrity making a scheduled appearance.
Heads turned.
Students walking between dorms and study halls instinctively glanced toward the sound of the engine.
More than a few already had their phones in hand, doomscrolling through clips from the game, and several lifted them almost automatically when the supercar passed.
Then they realized who was driving.
The reactions escalated immediately.
"Isn’t that the student tycoon’s Lamborghini?"
"STAN!"
"THAT’S HIM!"
"HUNDRED-YARD JUMPER, BABY!"
"PEAK!
Laughter followed.
A few students actually jogged alongside the sidewalk for several seconds trying to get a better look.
Stan simply raised a hand in acknowledgment without slowing down.
The gesture somehow made the crowd even more excited.
By the time he reached the dining hall, several people were already posting fresh photos online.
The building sat at the edge of the central commons, its large glass windows glowing warmly against the darkening evening.
Stan pulled into the visitor parking lot and guided the Huracán into a space near the entrance.
As the engine shut off, he glanced through the windshield and noticed that nearly every student passing by was slowing down to look at the car.
Several had already stopped entirely.
Two students were openly taking pictures.
One was recording a video.
Stan found himself mildly amused by the predictability of it all.
The Huracán had never been subtle.
He stepped out and locked the car.
Immediately, another small cluster of students started whispering.
The wide glass doors of the dining hall stood propped open.
Warm light spilled across the pavement.
Music drifted faintly from inside.
So did laughter.
The celebration was already well underway.
Just inside the entrance stood Zack.
The basketball captain had very obviously stationed himself there with one specific mission in mind.
Intercept Stan the moment he arrived.
The second he spotted him through the glass, his grin widened.
"Bro."
"Zack."
"You actually showed up in the Huracán."
"You sound surprised."
"I’m not surprised."
Zack pointed toward the parking lot behind him.
"I’m delighted."
He shook his head.
"The energy in there is already insane.
You pulling up in the matte-black is going to make it apocalyptic."
Stan considered that.
"That’s a strong word."
"It’s the correct word." Zack stepped forward, clapped him on the shoulder, and pulled him into a quick half-hug.
When he stepped back, he was still grinning.
"I don’t know if I told you this yet, but Zoey recorded everything."
"You mentioned it.
"The dunk clip just crossed eight million views."
Stan blinked.
"Eight?"
"Million." Zack held up a finger for emphasis.
"Eight.
Million."
A laugh escaped him.
"Zoey is one notification away from ascending into another plane of existence."
Then his expression softened slightly.
More genuine.
"Seriously, though."
He gestured toward the packed dining hall.
"Without you, none of this happens."
His voice carried a sincerity that cut through the jokes.
"We don’t beat Velaris Crown."
"We don’t bring the cup home."
"We don’t have half the campus celebrating tonight."
For a brief moment, Zack looked every bit the captain who had carried the hopes of the team all season.
Then the grin returned.
"So, on behalf of Peak University..."
He spread his arms dramatically.
"Thanks for casually deciding to become an elite basketball player for one afternoon."
Stan shrugged.
"You asked."
"I did."
"And somehow that’s still the craziest part."
Laughing, Zack turned toward the interior of the hall and began walking.
"Come on."
The noise grew louder with every step.
"The team’s at the back."
"The cheer squad’s here."
"Half the school is here."
He glanced over his shoulder.
"And approximately seventy percent of them are waiting to see if you’re actually real."
Stan followed him through the open doors.
Into the warmth.
Into the noise.
Into the celebration.
The team was waiting.
The cheer squad was waiting.
Sophie was waiting.
And the rest of the night was just beginning.

chapters.title: Chapter 263: The Girls’ Surprise
paragraphs: The moment Stan stepped into the venue, he was hit by a wall of loud, pulsing music that seemed to vibrate straight through his chest.

The space had been transformed into a full-blown celebration zone, colorful lights swept across the walls, tables overflowed with food and drinks, and students filled every corner, laughing, dancing, and basking in the glow of Peak University’s upset victory.
The bass carried real weight.
The kind of bass that traveled up through the floor and settled somewhere behind your sternum.
Stan couldn’t help nodding along to the beat as he walked inside, the adrenaline from the game still coursing through his veins.
Across the room, Zack spotted him first.
"Stan’s here!"

A cluster of basketball players occupied a high table in the corner, drinks already in hand and post-game excitement still written across their faces. Marcus saw him and immediately threw both arms into the air.
"MVP! MVP!"
The chant caught instantly.
"MVP! MVP! MVP!"
It spread from the table to the surrounding groups, and by the time Stan reached them, half the front section of the hall was cheering, whistling, or recording him on their phones.
He laughed and worked his way around the table, exchanging handshakes and shoulder bumps with each teammate, the practiced but genuine greetings of athletes who had just shared a huge win together.
Before he could sit down, Marcus shoved a glass into his hand.
Dark amber liquid.
Whiskey.
"Drink," Marcus declared. "Drink. You earned it three times over tonight."
Stan glanced at the glass. ’Well... one or two shots won’t hurt. Besides, my alcohol resistance is ridiculously high.’
One or two shots weren’t likely to accomplish much.
He took a sip. Then another. The whiskey was excellent. Dangerously excellent.
Smooth enough that he immediately understood why Marcus had looked so pleased with himself.
Stan lowered the glass. ’Okay. That was genuinely good whiskey.’
He opened his mouth to ask Marcus whether the cheer squad had arrived yet.
But then, his phone vibrated. Twice, almost simultaneously.
Stan frowned and pulled it from his pocket.
Two notifications sat at the top of the screen.
Both Snapchat. Both sent within the same minute. The first was from Maya.
Maya: [Stan, my love. Me and Sophie, who do you love most? Be honest.]
Stan blinked. Then opened the second.
Sophie: [My love, please tell me. Me and Maya, if you had to choose, who would you love more?]
For a moment, his brain simply stopped functioning.
Then he coughed. Once, sharp and unexpected.
Then again. The second cough was significantly worse.
Marcus immediately smacked him between the shoulder blades.
"Bro, you good?"
"Stan?" Zack suddenly appeared beside him. "You alright?"
The rest of the table had turned toward him as well. The concern was immediate and genuine.
After all, their newly crowned MVP appeared to be losing a fight against a glass of whiskey.
Stan held up one hand. "It’s fine."
Another cough escaped him. "It’s nothing."
Marcus looked unconvinced. Zack looked even less convinced. Stan cleared his throat and took a much more careful sip of whiskey.
"Wrong pipe."
"You sure?" Zack’s eyes narrowed slightly.
There was a texture to the question. The cough had not sounded like a wrong-pipe cough.
It had sounded suspiciously like a man receiving devastating information.
"I’m sure."
Zack studied him for another second. Then shrugged.
"If you say so."
At that exact moment, Zoey walked from somewhere within the crowd. She slipped an arm around Zack’s shoulders and leaned up to whisper something into his ear.
Whatever she said immediately made him laugh.
Just like that, Zack’s attention vanished.
Stan released a slow breath. Sighing, He unlocked his phone again and stared at the messages.
Then stared some more. The fact that they had arrived within the same minute felt deeply suspicious. Almost coordinated, possibly illegal.
’What in the actual hell is going on?’
He took another sip of whiskey, then began typing.
To Maya: [Well, what can I say? It’s hard to choose.]
Send.
To Sophie: [Well, what can I say? It’s hard to choose.]
Send.
Stan looked at the two conversations. Then looked up at the crowded dining hall.
Stan slipped the phone back into his pocket.
The problem with giving identical answers, he reflected, was that they usually only delayed the explosion.
Unfortunately for him, that realization arrived about three seconds too late.
Meanwhile, Both replies came back within seconds. Not minutes. Not even enough time to suggest they had paused to think. But seconds.
They had been typing almost the instant he hit send.
Maya: [Then rock and dance with Sophie at the party tonight ]
Stan blinked. He stared at the message for a moment before immediately switching to Sophie’s chat.
Stan: [What are you two up to?]
The reply arrived almost instantly.
Sophie: [What did Maya tell you?]
’Whats going on?!’ Stan’s eyes narrowed.
Stan: [That I should rock and dance with you.]
Three little dots appeared, disappeared then appeared again.
Then,
Sophie: [Good 🙂↕️]
Stan stared. He knew with that with their favourability being high, they were definitely his and his alone, but, he was dying of curiosity trying to think what their plan was
Stan: [What games are you two playing?]
Sophie: [Don’t worry, Stan. Nothing bad is going to happen. We’ve got a surprise for you tonight.]
A surprise. That somehow did not make him feel better.
He switched back to Maya’s chat.
Stan: [What are you two up to?]
Maya: [Don’t worry. It’s a surprise]
Stan looked at both conversations side by side. Then looked at them again.
His thumb hovered motionless above the screen while his face performed the tiny, controlled adjustments of a man desperately trying not to react in public.
Sophie and Maya were cooperating. Not tolerating each other, Not temporarily ignoring each other. But cooperating, actively, and deliberately.
Coordinating Snapchat messages down to the minute. That should not have been possible.
Unlike this, Sophie’s possessiveness, by Stan’s estimation, was normal. Maya’s competitive instinct toward Sophie was equally normal.
The two of them had spent most of the day operating like rival political parties campaigning for the same undecided voter.
They had ridden in the same car. They had smiled at him from opposite sides of the same space. They had flirted at him in alternating turns.
And they had avoided speaking directly to each other whenever possible.
Yet somehow, Now they were coordinating Snapchat messages.
Stan’s mind immediately began searching for explanations.
’What could have made them cooperate like this...’ He can understand their point of view but it still doesn’t make sense...
His thoughts abruptly hit a wall. ’No. That’s not the important question. The important question is why are they suddenly acting like co-conspirators?’

chapters.title: Chapter 264: Secret Understanding
paragraphs: Stan’s thoughts abruptly hit a wall. ’No. That’s not the important question. The important question is why are they suddenly acting like co-conspirators?’
That was significantly more alarming, though it was alarming in a good way since Stan was sure that this was to his benefit...
’Have they come to terms with each other as my girls,’ he sighed at this thought...
Maybe he should just stop stressing himself over this and let the girls do what they want...
Slowly, Stan lowered the phone and placed it face-up on the high table.
He stared into the middle distance.
"Well, I can’t wait to see what they planned..." The words escaped under his breath. Not loud enough for the surrounding music to swallow, but not quite quiet enough to be entirely private.
Marcus glanced over.
He hadn’t heard the words, but he was still concerned.
"Stan, bro." Marcus frowned. "Are you actually okay?"
"I’m okay."
"You don’t look okay."
"I’m okay."
"You look excited, well, what am I even saying, it’s only natural one would be so excited in a party."
Stan sighed, even though he didn’t care less about Marcus’ thoughts he still clarified; "I’m fine."
Marcus studied him for another second. Then shrugged. "Alright, man."
He took another drink and turned back toward the party.
Stan remained staring at his phone.
Based on his guess, he was pretty sure that somewhere in the crowd, Sophie and Maya were apparently planning a surprise together. He was not completely sure but that was what he thinks is going on.
And for reasons he couldn’t quite articulate, that fact was infinitely more terrifying than either of them acting alone.
Stan couldn’t help but get even more curious. ’These two cooperating? After all the tension earlier... this can’t be simple.’
Stan was halfway through his second whiskey and still trying to extract useful information from either chat when he noticed a hand waving at him from across the room.
He looked up.
Sophie stood beside one of the side tables near the edge of the dance floor.
For a moment, his entire train of thought regarding the mysterious Snapchat operation derailed as he fully registered what she was wearing.
She looked devastatingly sexy in that flashy party outfit, a tight, shimmering black mini dress that clung to every curve like liquid night.
The plunging neckline plunged daringly low, showcasing the deep valley of her full, heavy breasts that strained against the thin fabric with every breath.
The dress hugged her narrow waist before flaring over her wide hips and thick, juicy thighs, the hem barely covering the lower curve of her perfect ass.
Strappy heels accentuated her long legs, and her sleek black hair cascaded loosely over one shoulder. Light makeup made her eyes smolder with desire.
She caught his eye immediately. Then she smiled. Slowly, deliberately, she crooked a finger at him, signalling;
’Come please.’
Stan set his glass down on the high table.
"I’ll be back," he told Marcus.
Marcus glanced toward Sophie and immediately grinned. "Bro, take your time."
Stan ignored the look and started across the room.
The crowd seemed to part naturally as he moved through it. Some students recognized him and lifted their phones to record. Others called his name.
He paid none of them any attention. His focus remained fixed on Sophie.
Likewise, her attention never left him. By the time he reached her, the small pocket of space surrounding the table felt strangely private despite being only a few feet from a crowded dance floor.
Sophie was already pouring him a drink. A clean glass. Two fingers of something dark and expensive. Ice.
She handed it to him with the patient confidence of a woman who had known exactly where he would end up all evening.
Stan accepted it. Took a drink. Set the glass down.
Then leaned one hip against the table, studying her. "Where’s Maya?"
Sophie’s lips curved into a knowing smile. She didn’t glance away. Didn’t pretend not to understand the question.
She simply met his eyes directly. "Don’t worry about Maya."
"Sophie. You two sent me coordinated messages."
"Yes.."
"You’ve never coordinated with Maya about anything."
"True."
"So tell me, what’s happening, Sophie?"
She took a small sip from her own glass then et it down.

Then she reached forward and rested a hand lightly against his chest, over the fabric of his henley. The gesture was effortless, unhurried, dangerously romantic, the tension seemed to rise amidst the booming music around them.
"Just forget about how strange it looks tonight," she said softly, her voice barely carrying above the music. "Let’s have fun."
Stan narrowed his eyes. "Sophie."
"The least I can tell you," she continued, "is that we’re cooperating. We’ve talked. We’ve come to an understanding for tonight."
His eyebrows rose. "An understanding."
"Yes Stan."
"And that’s all you’re giving me."
"That’s all you need to know.
"And the surprise?"
Sophie’s smile deepened. "The surprise is the surprise. Trust me when I say you’ll love it. You’ll definitely enjoy the surprise we planned."
"Sophie."
"Stan." The way she said his name somehow managed to sound both affectionate and teasing.
"You’re going to enjoy yourself tonight," she said. "I promise."
For a long moment, he held her gaze. The system offered him absolutely nothing. No notification. No explanation. No convenient breakdown of whatever bizarre agreement Sophie and Maya had reached.
There was only Sophie’s hand resting lightly against his chest, her steady eyes, and her unwavering insistence that he stop worrying and trust her.
Stan turned the problem over one last time.
The most reasonable explanation, he decided, was that Maya hadn’t actually come.
Maybe the surprise was entirely Sophie’s idea.
Maybe Maya’s role had been limited to helping maintain the mystery through text.

Maya was practical. She might have decided that publicly sharing his attention with Sophie at a crowded campus party wasn’t something she was ready for yet and had quietly stepped aside for the evening.
The theory fit. It explained Sophie’s confidence. It explained her unusually relaxed mood.
It explained why Sophie seemed so certain he would enjoy himself.
Most importantly, it explained why Maya wasn’t standing here.
Satisfied enough, Stan finally let the question go. "Alright, I’m looking forward to this surprise you two are planned for me."
Sophie’s smile widened immediately. "Good, this might be really weird but it’s the best way forward for all of us."
"There you go speaking in parables again..."
She picked up her glass. "You’ll get what I mean soon, forget about that and drink with me."
Stan lifted his own. "Gladly."
"Eat with me."
"Easy enough."
"And dance with me when the music slows."
Something softer entered her expression. "It’s been a long time since we’ve had a proper dance together, my love."
For a moment, all of the mystery, confusion, and speculation faded into the background.
Stan smiled. "Alright, babe."
The smile Sophie gave him in return made it very clear she considered that the correct answer.

chapters.title: Chapter 275: System Upgrade
paragraphs: Stan waved them goodbye at the door of Maya’s apartment, the morning light still soft against the building’s exterior, then made the short walk to the parking area where he’d left the Huracán.
He slid into the driver’s seat, closed the door, and let out a long, slow sigh.
It had been a night.
For a moment, he simply sat there with both hands resting on the steering wheel, letting the quiet morning settle around him.
Then the system notifications began to appear.
[Ding!]
[Maya Zimmerman: Favorability has crossed 100]
[Ding!]
[Sophie Youngs: Favorability has crossed 125]
[Sophie Youngs, current favorability: 125]
Stan’s eyebrows rose.
A third notification followed almost immediately.
[Congratulations. You have brought a target’s favorability past the 120 threshold and unlocked the criteria for additional rewards.]
[Ding!]
[Hidden criteria triggered. System is upgrading.]
[Additional rewards will be issued once the system upgrade is complete.]
Stan stared at the floating notifications for several seconds.
Leaning back against the headrest, he reread them.
That was unexpected.

The 120-point threshold had been on his radar for days. When Amelia had first crossed one hundred favorability, the system had quietly hinted that another reward tier existed beyond it. Given her circumstances, a recovering coma patient who had awakened to discover that her rescuer was a billionaire shareholder who had personally spent thirty million dollars on her care, Stan had assumed she would be the first to reach it.
Apparently not. Sophie had hit 125. And she’d done it overnight.

Maya crossing 100 was almost as surprising. Her favorability had already been climbing steadily, but now the rate seemed to have accelerated dramatically. At this pace, she would likely break through 120 within days, perhaps even sooner.
Thinking back on it, the previous night had clearly carried far more emotional significance for both women than he had fully appreciated at the time.

For Sophie, it had represented a deliberate decision to set aside possessiveness and choose trust instead, a conscious choice to share rather than compete, made after her own private conversations with Maya.
For Maya, it had been something else entirely: validation. A long-delayed acknowledgment finally made real.
Whatever emotions each woman had brought into that night, they had both emerged from it feeling closer to him than before. The system’s metrics had registered that change immediately.
Still, the favorability increases weren’t what held his attention. The upgrade notification was. The system had never announced an upgrade before.
It had distributed rewards, enhanced his physique, improved his capabilities, and altered various aspects of his body, but it had always done so quietly, without fanfare.
This was different.

An explicit announcement, coupled with delayed rewards, suggested something more fundamental than another incremental improvement. It sounded less like an adjustment and more like a structural change.
Unfortunately, there was no way to know how long it would take.
He would simply have to wait.
Stan shook his head, pushed the thought aside, and started the engine.
The Huracán rumbled to life.
He had a meeting with Grayson.
The drive into central Inksea took a little under forty minutes.

The Wanhai Group’s Inksea branch occupied a sleek twenty-eight-story tower in the heart of the financial district, a clean glass-and-steel structure that anchored the eastern end of the city’s central commercial avenue.

Stan had passed the building countless times before he had ever set foot inside. He could still remember standing at a bus stop across the street months ago, staring up at the illuminated Wanhai logo and idly wondering what kind of people worked in a place like that.
Now he owned forty percent of it. The thought still caught him off guard occasionally.

He guided the Huracán into the executive parking level beneath the tower, a restricted section reserved for senior leadership and major shareholders. His credentials, issued within twenty-four hours of his ownership becoming public knowledge inside the company, opened the security gate automatically.
The parking level was quiet at this hour.
He pulled into a space between Grayson’s characteristically understated Bentley and an empty slot reserved, according to the plaque mounted beside it, for the Chief Operating Officer.
After locking the car, he headed for the executive elevator and rode it to the top floor.
There were two reasons he had come today; The first was simple: he wanted to see the branch for himself.

Over the past week, he had been making decisions about Wanhai based on reports, briefings, and Grayson’s summaries. He knew the numbers. He knew the organizational structure. He knew the strategic direction.
What he didn’t know was the building. The atmosphere. The people. The rhythm of day-to-day operations.
Everything he understood about the company had been filtered through someone else’s perspective. It was past time for a firsthand look.
The second reason was Grayson.
The older man had requested the meeting personally, and the wording of the request had caught Stan’s attention.
’I’d prefer to discuss this in person, at the branch.’
It wasn’t urgent enough for alarm. But it wasn’t casual, either.
The elevator chimed softly as it reached the top floor. The doors slid open. Stan stepped into the executive corridor.
Grayson’s assistant was already waiting.

A sharp, composed woman in her thirties, she carried herself with the effortless efficiency of someone who always seemed to know what was happening five minutes before everyone else. Given how quickly she appeared, she had almost certainly been notified the moment Stan’s vehicle entered the executive parking level.
She inclined her head politely.
"Mr. Harrison. Mr. Davies is expecting you."
"Thank you."
She gestured toward the corner office at the end of the corridor and opened the door as he approached.
Stan stepped inside. Grayson Davies rose from behind his desk.
As always, he looked like a man who had grown into wealth rather than been consumed by it. Mid-fifties. Silver beginning to creep through his hair at the temples.
Confident without being performative.
His charcoal-gray suit was impeccably tailored, but free of the loud excesses favored by men who relied on their clothing to announce their importance.
He extended a hand. A genuine smile followed, a rare expression reserved for people he respected rather than merely did business with.
"Stan."
"Grayson."
They shook hands.
"Sit," Grayson said. "I’ve had coffee brought up. We have a few things to discuss."
Stan took the chair opposite the desk.
Whatever Grayson had wanted to tell him, he was about to find out.
With that, the meeting began.

chapters.title: Chapter 276: The Cherry On Top
paragraphs: Grayson settled back in his chair, accepted the small porcelain coffee cup his assistant had placed at his elbow, and took a moment to choose his words carefully.

"Stan, before I get into this, I want to be upfront. What I’m about to discuss may feel like an intrusion into your personal life. I’d appreciate your patience while I explain why I felt it was something I needed to raise with you directly."
Stan set his own coffee down.
"Go ahead."
"It concerns Maya Zimmerman."
A slight crease formed between Stan’s brows.
"What about Maya?"

"I know the two of you are close. That’s hardly a secret. Between your work together on Ghost Signal, the publicity surrounding the film, and the countless photos and clips that have circulated over the past month, it’s widely understood, including by me, that there’s a personal connection between you. That’s why I’m bringing this to you instead of handling it quietly within Wanhai."
Stan met his gaze evenly.
"Is there something about Maya you want to tell me?"
Grayson let out a quiet breath through his nose.
"It feels strange even saying this aloud. As though I’ve somehow become a gossiping aunt instead of a senior executive. But before I proceed any further, I need you to clarify something."
"Then tell me."

"Maya approached me four days ago through her family’s connections. She brought me an investment proposal, and a proposal for a business partnership with the Wanhai Group." He paused briefly. "She’s planning to establish a cosmetics company."
Stan absorbed the information without any outward reaction.
"Are you bringing this up because her business would conflict with Wanhai’s cosmetics division?"

"At first glance, perhaps. But in reality, no. Even with the Zimmerman family’s backing, entering the market as a direct competitor would be extraordinarily difficult. Wanhai is a global operation. We could bury an early-stage startup like hers without even trying, not through malice, but simply through the weight of our market share." Grayson tilted his head slightly. "She understands that. She wouldn’t have come to me if she hadn’t done her homework."
"She studied the market carefully before approaching me. In fact, she structured her proposal specifically to avoid the obvious problem."
Reaching for a folder at the corner of his desk, Grayson slid it across to Stan.

"Her company intends to focus exclusively on the manufacturing side of the business. She has no plans to build her own retail or distribution network. That’s a deliberate decision, she’s positioning herself as a supplier, not a competitor. Wanhai’s cosmetics division, as you know, is built primarily around retail and distribution. The two ends of the chain don’t compete with each other. They complement one another."
Stan opened the folder and began turning the pages.

The proposal was clean and meticulously organized. The branding had clearly been handled by someone with a sharp eye for presentation, Maya’s aesthetic sense was evident on every page. The business model was tightly argued: specialized manufacturing, premium positioning, rigorous quality controls, and a clearly defined three-year expansion plan. The partnership structure offered Wanhai favorable supplier terms in exchange for access to its distribution network during the company’s formative years.
It was, Stan had to admit, genuinely impressive. Nodding, he continued turning the pages.
... Meanwhile, Grayson continued.

"My first instinct, when the proposal reached my desk, was to decline. Bringing a new supplier into a mature distribution network always creates friction. Existing suppliers, companies we’ve cultivated relationships with over decades, notice these things immediately. They interpret it as a hostile signal. And some of those relationships are worth far more to Wanhai than a single new supplier agreement."
"That’s the part you wanted to discuss with me."
"Part of it."
Stan closed the folder and placed it back on the desk. "And the other part?"
Grayson met his eyes.

"After reading the proposal in full, I realized I’d been looking at it the wrong way. If her company succeeds, and with the Zimmerman backing and what I’ve seen of her business sense, I now think it has a real chance, Wanhai stands to become one of its largest customers, not one of its competitors. Treating her as a threat today could shut the door on a partnership that might prove extremely valuable five or ten years from now."
"You’re inclined to take the deal."

"I’m inclined to consider it. The supplier friction is real and would have to be managed carefully. But the long-term upside is substantial enough that I felt I should speak with you before making any decision. Particularly given the personal dimension."

Stan considered that in silence. He hadn’t known about the cosmetics company. Maya had never mentioned it, not back at her apartment, nor during any of the half-dozen moments over the past two weeks when she easily could have.
Which meant she had made a deliberate choice.
She had built the proposal herself, approached Wanhai through her family’s channels, and structured the partnership without involving him.
The reason wasn’t difficult to guess.

Maya possessed a quiet independence that had become increasingly apparent since the Ghost Signal publicity campaign. For weeks, she had found herself constantly linked to him, professionally and personally, and Stan suspected she had wanted at least one major achievement that was wholly her own, something built with her own judgment rather than under his shadow.
That instinct wasn’t a rejection of him. If anything, it reflected her pride.
She loved him enough not to lean on him unnecessarily. She wanted to stand beside him, not behind him.
And perhaps she still wanted to prove something to herself. The question before him was a practical one.
"You said the supplier relationships are the real risk."
"Correct."
Grayson folded his hands together.

"Wanhai’s existing suppliers would view a new entrant backed by us as a threat. Some would lobby internally against the arrangement. Some might withdraw preferential terms. And a few would likely retaliate directly against Maya’s company through their own channels. Any of those outcomes would damage Wanhai’s broader supplier ecosystem."
Stan nodded slowly.

"So even though her company wouldn’t compete with Wanhai itself, it would compete with Wanhai’s other suppliers. And if those suppliers see Wanhai openly supporting her, they’ll view it as a betrayal of long-standing relationships. That damages Wanhai regardless of whether her company succeeds.
"Exactly." Grayson didn’t say anything further. He didn’t need to.
Stan could already see the shape of the recommendation Grayson was deliberately avoiding. So he voiced it himself.
"Then I’ll invest in her company instead."
Grayson blinked.
"Privately," Stan continued. "Anonymously. No public connection to Wanhai."
He tapped the folder lightly.

"If her venture succeeds, Wanhai can establish a supplier relationship later, organically, on the same terms as anyone else. If the company fails, or if complications arise, Wanhai’s name was never attached. The friction with our existing suppliers never materializes."
For the first time since the conversation had begun, Grayson’s shoulders relaxed noticeably.
"That was the structure I hoped you would arrive at, Sir Stan."
"You couldn’t suggest it directly."
"No." Grayson smiled faintly.
"Wanhai’s leverage is precisely what makes the partnership attractive to her. And Wanhai is the leverage we cannot extend without consequences."
"But I can."
"Exactly."

"As a private individual with substantial capital, you can provide the support she needs without entangling Wanhai’s reputation. You provide the financing. Her family’s connections handle the introductions. And when her company approaches Wanhai again, in three to five years, as an established supplier rather than an unproven startup, we can evaluate the relationship purely on its merits."
Stan tapped his finger lightly against the folder.
The deeper reason for his interest, of course, was the system.
Maya’s favorability had crossed one hundred that morning.
He had entered the ten-times rebate tier with her.

According to the projections in front of him, the venture would likely require eight to twelve million dollars in initial capital. Even setting sentiment aside, the rebate alone made the decision almost absurdly attractive. Whether the business ultimately flourished or failed, the numbers favored him.
The system had a curious way of bending his choices toward outcomes that benefited everyone involved.
Spend money on women whose favorability was high. Receive multiplied returns.
In this case, the alignment was almost embarrassing. The investment made sense even without the system. The system merely added a cherry on top.

The two ends of the chain don’t compete with each other.
They complement one another."
Stan opened the folder and began turning the pages.
The proposal was clean and meticulously organized.
The branding had clearly been handled by someone with a sharp eye for presentation, Maya’s aesthetic sense was evident on every page.
The business model was tightly argued: specialized manufacturing, premium positioning, rigorous quality controls, and a clearly defined three-year expansion plan.
The partnership structure offered Wanhai favorable supplier terms in exchange for access to its distribution network during the company’s formative years.
It was, Stan had to admit, genuinely impressive.
Nodding, he continued turning the pages.
Meanwhile, Grayson continued.
"My first instinct, when the proposal reached my desk, was to decline.
Bringing a new supplier into a mature distribution network always creates friction.
Existing suppliers, companies we’ve cultivated relationships with over decades, notice these things immediately.
They interpret it as a hostile signal.
And some of those relationships are worth far more to Wanhai than a single new supplier agreement."
"That’s the part you wanted to discuss with me."
"Part of it."
Stan closed the folder and placed it back on the desk.
"And the other part?"
Grayson met his eyes.
"After reading the proposal in full, I realized I’d been looking at it the wrong way.

If her company succeeds, and with the Zimmerman backing and what I’ve seen of her business sense, I now think it has a real chance, Wanhai stands to become one of its largest customers, not one of its competitors.
Treating her as a threat today could shut the door on a partnership that might prove extremely valuable five or ten years from now."
"You’re inclined to take the deal."
"I’m inclined to consider it.
The supplier friction is real and would have to be managed carefully.
But the long-term upside is substantial enough that I felt I should speak with you before making any decision.
Particularly given the personal dimension."
Stan considered that in silence.
He hadn’t known about the cosmetics company.
Maya had never mentioned it, not back at her apartment, nor during any of the half-dozen moments over the past two weeks when she easily could have.
Which meant she had made a deliberate choice.
She had built the proposal herself, approached Wanhai through her family’s channels, and structured the partnership without involving him.
The reason wasn’t difficult to guess.
Maya possessed a quiet independence that had become increasingly apparent since the Ghost Signal publicity campaign.

For weeks, she had found herself constantly linked to him, professionally and personally, and Stan suspected she had wanted at least one major achievement that was wholly her own, something built with her own judgment rather than under his shadow.
That instinct wasn’t a rejection of him.
If anything, it reflected her pride.
She loved him enough not to lean on him unnecessarily.
She wanted to stand beside him, not behind him.
And perhaps she still wanted to prove something to herself.
The question before him was a practical one.
"You said the supplier relationships are the real risk."
"Correct."
Grayson folded his hands together.
"Wanhai’s existing suppliers would view a new entrant backed by us as a threat.
Some would lobby internally against the arrangement.
Some might withdraw preferential terms.
And a few would likely retaliate directly against Maya’s company through their own channels.
Any of those outcomes would damage Wanhai’s broader supplier ecosystem."
Stan nodded slowly.
"So even though her company wouldn’t compete with Wanhai itself, it would compete with Wanhai’s other suppliers.
And if those suppliers see Wanhai openly supporting her, they’ll view it as a betrayal of long-standing relationships.
That damages Wanhai regardless of whether her company succeeds.
"Exactly." Grayson didn’t say anything further.
He didn’t need to.
Stan could already see the shape of the recommendation Grayson was deliberately avoiding.
So he voiced it himself.
"Then I’ll invest in her company instead."
Grayson blinked.
"Privately," Stan continued.
"Anonymously.
No public connection to Wanhai."
He tapped the folder lightly.
"If her venture succeeds, Wanhai can establish a supplier relationship later, organically, on the same terms as anyone else.
If the company fails, or if complications arise, Wanhai’s name was never attached.
The friction with our existing suppliers never materializes."
For the first time since the conversation had begun, Grayson’s shoulders relaxed noticeably.
"That was the structure I hoped you would arrive at, Sir Stan."
"You couldn’t suggest it directly."
"No." Grayson smiled faintly.
"Wanhai’s leverage is precisely what makes the partnership attractive to her.
And Wanhai is the leverage we cannot extend without consequences."
"But I can."
"Exactly."
"As a private individual with substantial capital, you can provide the support she needs without entangling Wanhai’s reputation.
You provide the financing.
Her family’s connections handle the introductions.
And when her company approaches Wanhai again, in three to five years, as an established supplier rather than an unproven startup, we can evaluate the relationship purely on its merits."
Stan tapped his finger lightly against the folder.
The deeper reason for his interest, of course, was the system.
Maya’s favorability had crossed one hundred that morning.
He had entered the ten-times rebate tier with her.
According to the projections in front of him, the venture would likely require eight to twelve million dollars in initial capital.
Even setting sentiment aside, the rebate alone made the decision almost absurdly attractive.
Whether the business ultimately flourished or failed, the numbers favored him.
The system had a curious way of bending his choices toward outcomes that benefited everyone involved.
Spend money on women whose favorability was high.
Receive multiplied returns.
In this case, the alignment was almost embarrassing.
The investment made sense even without the system.
The system merely added a cherry on top.

chapters.title: Chapter 277: Forty Percent Of An Empire
paragraphs: "I’ll invest in her company," Stan said. "Privately. No public association. Wanhai stays clean."
"Excellent."
"I’ll speak to her this afternoon. Once I’ve seen her numbers directly, you and I can work out the structure."
"Understood."
Grayson allowed himself a small, genuine smile.

"It’s been a pleasure discussing this with you, Stan. Most shareholders would have reacted one of two ways, they’d either dismiss the proposal outright or push Wanhai into a supplier conflict for the sake of short-term gains. You found the path that protects everyone."
"It’s the obvious solution."
Grayson chuckled softly. "It’s only obvious if you understand the supplier dynamics. Most people don’t. You’ve grasped Wanhai’s internal structure far more quickly than I expected."
Stan accepted the compliment with a slight inclination of his head and left it at that.
After the meeting, Grayson personally escorted him through the Wanhai branch.
The tour was unhurried and surprisingly thorough.

They moved through each of the major divisions in turn, corporate strategy, legal affairs, finance, commercial operations, and eventually the cosmetics division they had just been discussing. At each stop, Grayson introduced him to division heads and senior managers.
Most already knew him by name and face.

Some had attended the internal announcement Grayson had issued days earlier. Others had been present at the post-talent-show shareholders’ meeting and recognized him immediately. Regardless, everyone understood one fact clearly.
Stan was Wanhai’s largest individual shareholder.
The respect he received was measured rather than excessive, professional rather than fawning. Exactly as he preferred it.
What made him pause, however, was the brand wall in the central atrium. He slowed almost unconsciously.
Spread across the massive display were more than a hundred logos.
Consumer goods. Light manufacturing. Real estate. Hotels and hospitality. Beauty and cosmetics. Retail chains. Farming. Logistics. Financial services. And dozens of smaller specialized businesses.
Many of the brands were household names. Several enjoyed international recognition.
Wanhai lacked Star Entertainment’s dominance in any single industry, but the sheer breadth of its holdings placed it on comparable footing in terms of overall scale and influence.
Stan walked slowly along the wall.
For perhaps the first time since acquiring the shares, the meaning of forty percent of Wanhai Group ceased to be an abstract number.
Forty percent of this. Forty percent of companies that employed hundreds of thousands of people.
It’s been a while but still hard to come in terms after all this wasn’t just wealth. It was an ecosystem.
Standing a few paces behind him, Grayson watched in silence, wisely choosing not to interrupt.
Eventually, Stan resumed walking.

Employees greeted him with polite professionalism as they passed. He acknowledged each greeting with a brief nod and moved on. He wasn’t there to perform or cultivate popularity. He was there to observe.
And observe he did.
By the time the tour concluded, he understood Wanhai’s rhythm far better than he had after two weeks of reports and briefings. Numbers on paper could only convey so much.
Seeing the organization in motion was different.
At the executive elevator bank, he shook Grayson’s hand. "Thank you."
"My pleasure, Stan."
The elevator doors slid shut.
As the car descended toward the private parking level, Stan found himself thinking not about percentages or valuations, but about responsibility.
Forty percent. The number had sounded impressive when he first heard it.
Now, after walking through the living machinery behind it, it felt heavy.
Not unpleasantly so. Just real.
In the Huracán, before pulling out of the parking bay, Stan brought up Maya’s contact on his phone.
He paused for a moment, considering how to begin.
He could have opened with something softer, a teasing remark, a good morning, the easy warmth between two people who had spent the previous night together.
But what he wanted to discuss was too important to bury beneath pleasantries.
Maya valued directness.
She’d appreciate honesty more than performance. He typed.
Stan: [Maya. I just left Grayson at Wanhai’s Inksea branch. He briefed me on your cosmetics company. Why didn’t you tell me about this?]
He sent the message.
The typing indicator appeared almost immediately.
Thirty seconds later, her reply came.
Maya: [Oh you know Grayson...]
Stan: [Is it that surprising...]
Maya: [Well with your standing it’s not surprising, but it still came as a shocker to me...]
Maya: [I’m sorry. I didn’t mean for you to find out that way.]
Maya: [I wasn’t trying to hide it from you.]

Maya: [After everything you’ve already done for me, the Ghost Signal screenplay, the studio deal, the development funding, you’ve done so much, Stan. I have enough capital to get started. I wasn’t desperate for money.]
Another message followed.
Maya: [I approached Wanhai because I needed influence in the cosmetics industry and, eventually, access to a distribution network. That’s something I couldn’t get anywhere else.]
Maya: [And I’ve said it before... I didn’t want to become the woman who’s always asking you for things.]
Stan read the messages twice. The honesty in them was unmistakable. Maya wasn’t scrambling for an excuse. She was telling him the truth.
He had read her correctly. Her independence wasn’t pride born of distrust. It was pride born of self-respect.
She wanted to build something that belonged to her. Something with Maya Zimmerman written on it. Not something people would dismiss as another gift from Stan.
And she had deliberately gone through her family’s channels to avoid creating a visible line back to him.
He respected that. It was one of the reasons he loved her. But independence and partnership weren’t opposites. He typed again.
Stan: [I understand. And I respect the instinct. But here’s what’s actually happening.]

Stan: [If Wanhai openly supports your company, it creates problems with their existing suppliers. Grayson can’t take that risk. The partnership you envisioned isn’t impossible, but it can’t happen right now, not through Wanhai directly.]
Stan: [But I can invest privately. No public connection to Wanhai. No complications. You get support without putting Wanhai into a supplier conflict.]
Stan: [And when your company has established itself in a few years, Wanhai can approach you as they would any proven supplier.]
A few seconds passed.
Then he sent another message.
Stan: [I want to see the entire prospectus. Send it to me on Snapchat. Numbers, projections, sourcing, manufacturing plans, everything. Don’t leave anything out.]
The typing indicator reappeared.
Maya: [Stan, I—]
Then, after several seconds,
Maya: [Okay.]
Another message.
Maya: [Thanks.]
Then:
Maya: [You’re right about the supplier dynamic. I didn’t think that part through completely. I should have.]
Maya: [I’ll send everything tonight. The full prospectus. Financial projections. Sourcing breakdowns. Manufacturing partners. Everything.]
Maya: [You’ll have it before the end of the evening.]
And then:
Maya: [Thank you.]
Maya: [Not just for taking it seriously.]
Maya: [Thank you for not stepping in and taking it away from me.]
Stan smiled faintly.
His fingers moved over the keyboard.
Stan: [I’d never take it away from you, Maya.]
Stan: [I want to help. That’s different.]
The reply came almost instantly.
Maya: [I know.]
Maya: [That’s why I’m sending it.]
Maya: [💕]
The smile lingered. He slipped the phone into his pocket, pressed the ignition button, and listened as the Huracán came to life beneath him.
As he eased out of the parking bay, he reflected that the morning had been unexpectedly productive.
He had gained a much clearer understanding of Wanhai.
He had identified a promising private investment. He had preserved Maya’s independence while finding a way to support her.
And somewhere at the back of his mind lingered the unanswered question of the system upgrade and whatever changes were still taking shape behind the scenes.
Not bad for a single morning.
Stan drove out into the sunlight of Inksea with the quiet satisfaction of a man who had advanced several pieces on the board before noon.
And the day was still young.

chapters.title: Chapter 278: An Unexpected Convoy
paragraphs: Stan drove with one hand on the wheel, the other resting on his thigh as he idly checked his phone while waiting at a red light.
A Snapchat from Vivian sat at the top of his notifications.

This one was different from the usual professional updates she sent him in his capacity as her superior. The tone was personal, almost desperate. It had been typed in one long, breathless burst, the kind that signaled genuine distress rather than performative drama.

Vivian: [Sir Stan. I need your guidance. Von wasted far more of the family inheritance than any of us realized, far, far more. The scammer didn’t just take what Von handed over. He had Von signing transfers and authorizations for weeks. The damage is severe. And now that it’s becoming clear how much we’ve lost, the Reeves family’s longtime competitors are starting to circle. People we considered allies for years, old family friends, business partners my father trusted, they’re moving on us. I can’t tell which of them are still safe and which ones are wolves in sheep’s clothing. I genuinely can’t tell, Sir Stan. They smile when they talk to me and I can feel the knives behind their teeth. I don’t know who I can trust anymore.]
Stan read the message twice and let out a slow breath as the light turned green.
He eased the Huracán forward.

Truthfully, he had little desire to help the Reeves family. Von had brought the disaster on himself. By any fair assessment, the collapse of the Reeves’ position was the inevitable consequence of a spoiled heir refusing to listen to the one person who had tried to stop him. Vivian had told him the picture on his phone was AI-generated. She had warned him repeatedly.
He hadn’t listened. Even though the warning came to late, the fact that he didn’t discuss this with anyone before making this move made it clear that he had earned the outcome.
But there was a second dimension to the matter, one that concerned Stan far more.
The man who had scammed Von had been posing as Sir Streak. And this wasn’t the first time.

Damien had pulled the same stunt about close to two weeks earlier, and Stan had dealt with him personally at the Wanhai Grand. Now there was another impersonator, operating on a much larger scale, running elaborate long cons against inherited wealth using a counterfeit version of his identity.
And if there were two, there were almost certainly more. Probably many more.
Spread across different cities. Different platforms. Different circles.
Each one represented a small but very real threat to the actual Streak’s reputation.
It was time to address the problem properly.
He had been turning the matter over in the back of his mind for days. The same answer kept presenting itself.
Vanguard. The team that had escorted Amelia had been deeply unimpressive, patchwork, undertrained, and embarrassingly slow to react.
But that had been a consequence of the assignment, not the company itself.

Amelia had insisted on female-only protection, forcing Vanguard to cobble together a unit by pulling women from multiple teams. Individually, the guards had been competent. Collectively, they had lacked cohesion.
The company itself, however, was another matter entirely.

The Inksea Police Commissioner had spoken highly of Vanguard Protection Group, and he was not a man who handed out praise lightly. His comments had made it clear that when Vanguard operated at full capability, it was exceptionally good at what it did, and what it did extended far beyond executive protection.
The firm possessed a serious intelligence and investigative arm.
They specialized in finding people who did not want to be found.
Which made them perfectly suited to the problem.
Stan made a mental note.

Once he got home, he would conduct a proper review of Vanguard. If the company checked out, he would quietly retain them to track down the scammer who had fleeced Von and, more importantly, to identify every other Streak impersonator operating across TikTuk and the offline circuits.
Find them, expose them. And perhaps make a very public example of one or two.
That alone would be enough to send a message.
Sir Streak was not an identity that could be borrowed casually.
The Reeves family would benefit as a side effect.
Stan himself would benefit considerably more. He slipped the phone back into his pocket and returned his attention to the road.
The drive back to Aurelia Heights was uneventful.
He was perhaps three minutes from the building, already turning onto the residential approach that led to the underground parking entrance, when he spotted them.
A line of vehicles stood parked neatly along the curb outside the main gate.
Five cars.
Polished. Professional. Arranged with the kind of deliberate spacing that spoke of protocol rather than convenience.
The lead vehicle bore a familiar silver-on-black insignia on its rear quarter panel.
Vanguard Protection Group.
Stan slowed. "What the fuck?"
He spoke the words quietly to the empty cabin. His mind did the math immediately.
’Vanguard. Five cars...’
There was exactly one Vanguard client he knew who traveled with a five-car convoy.
’Amelia Don.’
Stan let out a long, measured sigh.
"Why does she have to make a show of this?" he muttered. "It looks like I’m a wanted criminal."
The timing was almost absurd.

He had been thinking about Vanguard less than half an hour ago, considering whether to hire them himself. And now their most high-profile client was parked outside his apartment building with an armed security detail.
Frankly, it would have been funny if it wasn’t so conspicuous.
He eased the Huracán to a stop in front of the gate, lowered his window, and waited.
The rear door of the lead sedan, a sleek black executive car, opened. Amelia stepped out.

She wore a tailored cream coat over a darker ensemble beneath, the lines clean and understated in the way that truly expensive clothes tended to be. There was nothing flashy about her appearance. Real wealth rarely needed to announce itself.

Her dark hair had been gathered into a low, elegant knot at the nape of her neck. A pair of black-framed sunglasses rested on her face, not the oversized fashion variety, but a slimmer, sharper design that lent her a reserved, almost austere air, as though she had decided that being recognized today was entirely beside the point.
She looked, in a word, beautiful.
The severity of the aesthetic only enhanced the effect.

The sunglasses concealed just enough of her eyes to draw attention elsewhere, to the graceful line of her jaw, the soft curve of her lips, and the quiet composure that seemed to permeate her every movement. There was something effortlessly refined about her, a kind of restrained elegance that made loud displays seem unnecessary.
[Reference Image]

Which made them perfectly suited to the problem.
Stan made a mental note.
Once he got home, he would conduct a proper review of Vanguard.

If the company checked out, he would quietly retain them to track down the scammer who had fleeced Von and, more importantly, to identify every other Streak impersonator operating across TikTuk and the offline circuits.
Find them, expose them.
And perhaps make a very public example of one or two.
That alone would be enough to send a message.
Sir Streak was not an identity that could be borrowed casually.
The Reeves family would benefit as a side effect.
Stan himself would benefit considerably more.
He slipped the phone back into his pocket and returned his attention to the road.
The drive back to Aurelia Heights was uneventful.
He was perhaps three minutes from the building, already turning onto the residential approach that led to the underground parking entrance, when he spotted them.
A line of vehicles stood parked neatly along the curb outside the main gate.
Five cars.
Polished.
Professional.
Arranged with the kind of deliberate spacing that spoke of protocol rather than convenience.
The lead vehicle bore a familiar silver-on-black insignia on its rear quarter panel.
Vanguard Protection Group.
Stan slowed.
"What the fuck?"
He spoke the words quietly to the empty cabin.
His mind did the math immediately.
’Vanguard.
Five cars...’
There was exactly one Vanguard client he knew who traveled with a five-car convoy.
’Amelia Don.’
Stan let out a long, measured sigh.
"Why does she have to make a show of this?" he muttered.
"It looks like I’m a wanted criminal."
The timing was almost absurd.
He had been thinking about Vanguard less than half an hour ago, considering whether to hire them himself.
And now their most high-profile client was parked outside his apartment building with an armed security detail.
Frankly, it would have been funny if it wasn’t so conspicuous.
He eased the Huracán to a stop in front of the gate, lowered his window, and waited.
The rear door of the lead sedan, a sleek black executive car, opened.
Amelia stepped out.
She wore a tailored cream coat over a darker ensemble beneath, the lines clean and understated in the way that truly expensive clothes tended to be.
There was nothing flashy about her appearance.
Real wealth rarely needed to announce itself.
Her dark hair had been gathered into a low, elegant knot at the nape of her neck.

A pair of black-framed sunglasses rested on her face, not the oversized fashion variety, but a slimmer, sharper design that lent her a reserved, almost austere air, as though she had decided that being recognized today was entirely beside the point.
She looked, in a word, beautiful.
The severity of the aesthetic only enhanced the effect.

The sunglasses concealed just enough of her eyes to draw attention elsewhere, to the graceful line of her jaw, the soft curve of her lips, and the quiet composure that seemed to permeate her every movement.
There was something effortlessly refined about her, a kind of restrained elegance that made loud displays seem unnecessary.

chapters.title: Chapter 279: The Heiress Who Waited All Night
paragraphs: She looked insanely beautiful, but despite the convoy, the bodyguards, and the carefully maintained seriousness she wore like armor, the sight of her stepping out to meet him carried a strangely simple implication.
Amelia Don had come here personally. Which meant whatever had brought her to his place wasn’t business that could be delegated. And it was pretty obvious what it was.

The doors of the four cars behind her opened in perfect, coordinated sequence. Eight armed female guards stepped out and spread into a loose but disciplined formation behind her. Stan recognized Emma at the front of the group, the leader of the original detail, looking far more composed and confident than she had at the abandoned building.
Amelia raised a single hand and the entire formation stopped instantly.

She didn’t want this to feel like an act of intimidation. She didn’t want him to think she had come looking for trouble. If anything, she wanted the opposite. But she also knew that a man who had broken through a steel door and disabled six armed kidnappers in twelve seconds was not someone who would be intimidated by a few bodyguards. The display was for the people watching around them, not for him.
Leaving the guards where they stood, she walked toward the Huracán alone.
She reached the driver’s side window and looked inside.
Stan looked back at her. For a moment, she simply stood there, taking him in.

The man behind the wheel was the same man whose photograph she had memorized while lying in her hospital bed, but the picture hadn’t captured him properly. It had shown a young executive at a corporate event, polished, ordinary, forgettable.
The man sitting in the Huracán was something else entirely.

He seemed settled. Alert. Watching her without any of the defensive habits she had spent her entire life learning to recognize in men. His expression was calm. His eyes steady. He regarded her with the quiet curiosity of someone studying a complicated puzzle that had unexpectedly arrived at his gate.
’I’ve finally met him.’
The thought came with a slow, warm certainty, carrying the weight of emotions that had been building inside her for days.
’The man who saved my life.’
He looked even more handsome in person than in the photos she had stared at for hours on her phone. Before she could stop herself, a small, gentle smile touched her lips.
At that exact moment, Stan’s vision filled with notifications.
[Amelia Don: Favorability 115 → 120]
[Amelia Don: Favorability 120 → 126]
[Ding!]
[You have fulfilled the conditions for additional rewards.]
[Amelia Don has surpassed the 125 Favorability threshold.]
Stan, outwardly, showed no reaction. Internally, he was briefly stunned.

The last time he had checked, Amelia’s favorability had been sitting at 115, climbing steadily but slowly. Thirty seconds of standing face-to-face with him had pushed it past 120 and all the way to 126.
While he didn’t know about this but whatever effect his photograph had had on her hospital bed, the reality of meeting him in person was proving considerably more potent.
He kept his expression composed and spoke first; "How long have you been waiting out here, Miss Amelia?"
The question was casual. The implication, that her impressive convoy had clearly been parked outside his gate for quite some time, was considerably less subtle.
Amelia coughed softly into her closed hand.

It was the small, half-deliberate sort of cough people used to buy themselves a moment when caught off guard. She could already feel a faint warmth creeping up the back of her neck, and she knew that even behind her sunglasses, it was probably noticeable.
’What would he think of me if he knew I’d spent the entire night waiting out here? No. I can’t answer that question.’
She was absolutely not answering that question.
Straightening her shoulders, she chose to deflect.
"How long I’ve been waiting isn’t important." Her voice remained steady, though quieter than she intended. "What’s important is that you saved my life. I owe you a great deal, Sir Stan."
Stan let the deflection pass without comment.
"That’s a generous way to put it." His gaze flicked briefly toward the assembled convoy. "Although the setup out here does make it look like I’ve done something deeply wrong."
She blinked. Then, to her own embarrassment, she glanced over her shoulder at the line of vehicles and guards.
"That’s exactly why I think we should have this conversation somewhere less..." She made a vague gesture at the spectacle behind her. "Formal."
A hint of color touched her cheeks.
"Coffee. Breakfast. Somewhere we can actually talk.
Stan’s lips curved into a slow, amused smile. Locking eyes with her through the open window, he asked;
"Are you asking me out, Miss Amelia?"
Amelia coughed again. Harder this time. She turned her head away for a moment to recover her composure as the warmth rising up her neck spread visibly to her cheeks.
’Is he teasing me? Is he flirting? Or does he just talk this casually about things like this?’ She had no idea.
And worse, she had no idea how she was supposed to know.

The truth was that her vocabulary for this sort of exchange was woefully underdeveloped. She had spent her entire adult life avoiding precisely this register of conversation with men. She had no memories to draw on. No experiences to reference. No practiced responses waiting in reserve.
What she did know was that he had just called her out for asking him out, and she was...
With a small, distant sense of horror, she realized she was blushing.

She had never blushed in front of a man before. Not once. The closest she had ever come had been the cold, controlled flush of anger she’d felt at fourteen when one of her uncles had leaned far too close into her personal space. That had been blood under pressure.
This... This was something else. This was warmth.
And she had absolutely no idea what to do with warmth.
[Amelia Don: Favorability 126 → 128]
Stan watched the delicate color climb across her face and, for once, decided to be merciful.
"Alright, Miss Amelia. I accept your offer."
He tilted his head toward the opposite side of the street.
"There’s a small restaurant over there. No need to drive." His smile deepened slightly. "We can walk."
Amelia nodded immediately.
