chapters.title: Chapter 280: No, Amelia
paragraphs: Stan pulled the Huracán smoothly into his private parking bay, stepped out, and met her at the curb. The Vanguard guards followed at a discreet distance, close enough to maintain their protective perimeter, far enough not to intrude.
Emma resumed her place at the front, carrying the quiet alertness of a captain who had finally learned that her job was protection, not performance.

The restaurant across the street was a quiet, well-kept place that catered mostly to the building’s residents. It specialized in early breakfasts and morning coffee, serving executives rushing off to work alongside regulars who arrived at the same time every day. It was open. Civilized. Neutral ground.
Exactly what they both needed.

As they entered, the hostess recognized him immediately, he had eaten there often enough, and led them to a secluded corner booth without comment. She spared only a brief glance toward the female guards quietly occupying nearby tables before making the professional decision not to ask questions.
Amelia slid into the booth opposite him. Stan took the seat across from her.
A small smile softened her face.
"While I know you can certainly take care of yourself, Sir Stan, this meal is on me. It’s the least I can do."
"It’s coffee, Amelia." He picked up the menu, glanced at it, then set it back down. "I’d argue about it, but I’d lose."
A faint smile touched his lips.
"And by the way, you can drop the Sir. It’s just Stan."
She inclined her head. "Stan."
She repeated the name carefully, almost experimentally, as though trying out a new language. The sound carried a strange, quiet intimacy that settled somewhere inside her chest and refused to leave.
The waiter arrived. Stan ordered a flat white and an omelette.
Amelia ordered black coffee and a fruit plate, the choice of someone who had spent days eating hospital food and was easing herself back toward normal life.
The waiter departed. And the air between them settled.
To Amelia’s quiet astonishment... It was comfortable.
She hadn’t prepared for this.

She had spent the entire sleepless night outside his gate rehearsing for awkwardness. For strained politeness. For resentment. Perhaps even hostility. A man whose life she had invaded had every right to be irritated by her ambush.

Instead, she found herself sitting across from him in a quiet corner booth, morning sunlight catching the edge of his face, waiting for coffee she hadn’t realized she wanted, and experiencing something entirely foreign.
For the first time in her adult life, being alone with a man in a small, enclosed space did not feel like something she needed to brace herself against.
And perhaps even stranger... She realized she had never truly felt comfortable with another person at all.
Her friendships were transactional. Her business relationships carefully managed. Her romantic life was not a tragedy or a disappointment.
It was simply an absence. Structured. Intentional and empty.
Yet here she was, seated across from a man she had properly met less than five minutes ago, feeling as though the morning itself had slowed for her.
As though, for the first time in years, she could breathe at the same pace as the world around her.
No expectations. No calculations. No walls. Just a quiet booth.
Morning sunlight. Coffee on the way. And him.
She looked across the table. Stan looked back at her with the same calm, attentive expression.
Amelia drew in a gentle breath.
Then, deciding there was no point delaying any longer... She began.
But just as she was about to begin the waiter came and set their drinks down. The flat white in front of Stan. The black coffee in front of Amelia. The fruit plate would follow in a few minutes.
Amelia wrapped her fingers around the warm cup but didn’t drink. She looked at Stan across the table for a long moment, gathering her thoughts, and then began carefully.

"Stan. Before anything else, I need you to understand something about me." Her voice was steady, but quieter than it had been outside. "I don’t look like it. I know I don’t. The cars, the guards, the way I move through the world, none of that makes me look like a woman who takes debt seriously. But I do. I take debt and gratitude more seriously than most people I’ve met."
She paused, choosing the next words deliberately.

"My mother taught me that. Before everything else fell apart, that’s the one thing she made sure I carried forward. If someone helps you, you remember it. If someone saves you, you spend the rest of your life finding a way to repay it. I’ve never forgotten that. I have never owed anyone anything I haven’t returned tenfold, and I have never accepted a kindness without finding the way to honor it."
Stan watched her without interrupting.

"You saved my life." Her eyes met his squarely. "You paid for my treatment when you had no reason to. You walked away without leaving a name, and you made sure the hospital wouldn’t give me one. That is not, that is not a debt I can carry without trying to repay it. I won’t be at peace until I’ve done something."
She took a small breath.

"I want to pay you back. Every dollar of the thirty million you spent on the elite protocol. And more, significantly more, beyond the treatment cost. Whatever number reflects what I owe for the life-saving itself. I’ve already calculated several figures and none of them feel sufficient, because the truth is..." Her voice softened. "The truth is no amount of money is genuinely enough. My life is worth more than money. That’s what makes this difficult to settle. But I’m asking you to let me try."
She looked at him with the steady, almost solemn expression of a woman who had been preparing this speech for two days and was delivering it exactly the way she had rehearsed.
Stan held her gaze for a beat. Then he shook his head slowly.
"No, Amelia."
She blinked. "No?"

chapters.title: Chapter 281: Consider It Done
paragraphs: "No, Amelia."
She blinked. "No?"
"I don’t want repayment. Not for the treatment. Not for anything."
Amelia stared at him.
The refusal had been delivered cleanly and without hesitation, with the same calm certainty he used for every statement he made. It was not a negotiating position. It was a finished answer.
For a moment she didn’t know what to say.

She had, on some level, been half-expecting this. The way he had handled everything from the moment she had woken up suggested it. He had not left his name. He had not left contact information. He had specifically, she had learned from the hospital’s compliance officer, instructed the facility to never release his account details to any patient or representative. Every signal he had transmitted since the rescue had been the signal of a man who did not want repayment.

Which meant her instinct had been correct. Which meant the speech she had prepared, in some part of her mind, had always been a speech she would have to deliver against an opponent who had already declined to participate in the exchange.
She set her coffee down.

"I was half-expecting that, honestly." Her voice carried a small, quiet acknowledgment. "Especially after I learned what you’d done with the hospital. Most people who help anonymously don’t go to the trouble of staying anonymous afterward. You did. That told me a lot."
She drew a slow breath.

"If you weren’t who you are, if you weren’t a public figure right now, with your face on every TikTuk feed and your name on every viral clip, finding you would have been almost impossible. I want you to know I would have tried anyway. I would have spent however long it took. But the fact that you’re already this visible is the only reason I didn’t have to spend the next two years looking."
She took the smallest sip of her coffee.

"So tell me." Her eyes lifted to his again, steady and serious. "You really don’t want any repayment? You don’t need my help with anything? Nothing I have, money, influence, connections, anything, is something you want from me?"
Stan watched her.

He had been about to give her the same straight no he gave to most of these questions. The system penalty made the refusal automatic, if she returned the thirty million, the hundred-times multiplier would shred him for three billion dollars he did not currently have available in liquid form.
But the second half of her question landed differently than the first.
’You don’t need my help with anything?’
The answer to that was, suddenly, not no.

Amelia Don was a Warner Bros. shareholder with significant international reach. Amelia Don had a personal security detail from Vanguard, the same firm Stan had been considering hiring less than an hour ago. Amelia Don had connections he didn’t have, in industries he wasn’t yet established in, with access points he couldn’t directly buy.
And Amelia Don was, by her own urgent insistence, looking for a way to repay him that wasn’t money.
He set his coffee down.
"Since you’re so determined to find a way," he said quietly, "there is something."

Amelia’s eyes lit up. The change was instant and unmistakable, the visible relief of a woman who had spent two days carrying a debt she couldn’t put down and had just been given permission to start carrying it differently.
"Anything," she said. "Name it."

"I’ve been dealing with a problem for the past several weeks." He kept his voice level. "A number of people have been impersonating me. Not casually, systematically. Some of them on platforms, posing as me online. Some of them in person, presenting themselves to wealthy targets as me and running long cons. One of them recently scammed the heir of the Reeves family, a young man named Von Reeves, out of a substantial portion of his inheritance. The scammer used my online alias to do it. Specifically, he used my identity as Sir Streak."
Amelia’s brow tightened. She was listening with the focused, calculating attention of a woman whose business instincts had just kicked in.

"I’ve been thinking about the right way to handle it," Stan continued. "It’s not a problem I can solve through public confrontation, exposing one impersonator publicly just teaches the rest to be more careful. What I need is a coordinated tracking operation. Someone who can identify the scammers operating under my identity across multiple platforms and multiple geographies, and then make them pay in a way that sends a clear, lasting message to everyone else considering it."
He held her eye.

"You have Vanguard on retainer. Vanguard has a serious intelligence and tracking division, I’ve been told as much, by people whose judgment I trust. You also have the broader Warner Bros. network and your own connections beyond it. Between Vanguard and your own resources, you have the ability to find these people and dismantle their operations in a way I can’t easily do on my own."
He let the proposition settle.

"Track them. Identify the active impersonators. Get the man who scammed Von Reeves first, that one is personal to me, and I want him made into a public example. And after that, the rest. Systematically. Quietly. Until the world understands that pretending to be Sir Streak is not something that goes unanswered."
He sat back slightly.
"That’s what I want. If you genuinely want to repay me, that’s the help I’ll take."
Amelia did not respond immediately.

She held the cup in her hands and looked at him across the table with the careful, measured stillness of a woman processing an offer she had not been expecting. The fruit plate arrived. The waiter set it down between them without comment and left.
Neither of them touched it.
Amelia exhaled slowly.
"You’re asking me," she said, "to use Vanguard and my Warner Bros. influence to run a coordinated international tracking operation against organized identity fraud."
"Yes."
"Targeting scammers operating across multiple platforms in multiple jurisdictions."
"Yes."
"With the explicit goal of making at least one of them a public example severe enough to deter the rest."
"Yes."
A small, slow smile began to form at the corner of her mouth.

It was not a polite smile. It was not the careful, neutral smile she had used in the parking lot earlier. It was something sharper and more focused, the expression of a woman who had spent her adult life building and using her influence in opposition to predators, who had a long, well-established personal hatred of men who took from those weaker than them, and who had just been handed a project that aligned, almost perfectly, with the most satisfying impulses she carried.
"Stan." Her voice was quieter now, but it had gained a new edge. "Do you understand what you’re asking?"
"I think I do."
"You’re asking me to do the one type of work I genuinely enjoy. The one type. Tracking down men who exploit other people’s trust and dismantling them. Publicly."
"I had a feeling you might be the right person for it."
She held his eye for a long moment.
Then she set her cup down with deliberate care.
"Consider it done."

sentences.text: "No, Amelia."
She blinked.
"No?"
"I don’t want repayment.
Not for the treatment.
Not for anything."
Amelia stared at him.
The refusal had been delivered cleanly and without hesitation, with the same calm certainty he used for every statement he made.
It was not a negotiating position.
It was a finished answer.
For a moment she didn’t know what to say.
She had, on some level, been half-expecting this.
The way he had handled everything from the moment she had woken up suggested it.
He had not left his name.
He had not left contact information.
He had specifically, she had learned from the hospital’s compliance officer, instructed the facility to never release his account details to any patient or representative.
Every signal he had transmitted since the rescue had been the signal of a man who did not want repayment.
Which meant her instinct had been correct.
Which meant the speech she had prepared, in some part of her mind, had always been a speech she would have to deliver against an opponent who had already declined to participate in the exchange.
She set her coffee down.
"I was half-expecting that, honestly." Her voice carried a small, quiet acknowledgment.
"Especially after I learned what you’d done with the hospital.
Most people who help anonymously don’t go to the trouble of staying anonymous afterward.
You did.
That told me a lot."
She drew a slow breath.
"If you weren’t who you are, if you weren’t a public figure right now, with your face on every TikTuk feed and your name on every viral clip, finding you would have been almost impossible.
I want you to know I would have tried anyway.
I would have spent however long it took.
But the fact that you’re already this visible is the only reason I didn’t have to spend the next two years looking."
She took the smallest sip of her coffee.
"So tell me." Her eyes lifted to his again, steady and serious.
"You really don’t want any repayment?
You don’t need my help with anything?
Nothing I have, money, influence, connections, anything, is something you want from me?"
Stan watched her.
He had been about to give her the same straight no he gave to most of these questions.

The system penalty made the refusal automatic, if she returned the thirty million, the hundred-times multiplier would shred him for three billion dollars he did not currently have available in liquid form.
But the second half of her question landed differently than the first.
’You don’t need my help with anything?’
The answer to that was, suddenly, not no.
Amelia Don was a Warner Bros. shareholder with significant international reach.
Amelia Don had a personal security detail from Vanguard, the same firm Stan had been considering hiring less than an hour ago.
Amelia Don had connections he didn’t have, in industries he wasn’t yet established in, with access points he couldn’t directly buy.
And Amelia Don was, by her own urgent insistence, looking for a way to repay him that wasn’t money.
He set his coffee down.
"Since you’re so determined to find a way," he said quietly, "there is something."
Amelia’s eyes lit up.

The change was instant and unmistakable, the visible relief of a woman who had spent two days carrying a debt she couldn’t put down and had just been given permission to start carrying it differently.
"Anything," she said.
"Name it."
"I’ve been dealing with a problem for the past several weeks." He kept his voice level.
"A number of people have been impersonating me.
Not casually, systematically.
Some of them on platforms, posing as me online.
Some of them in person, presenting themselves to wealthy targets as me and running long cons.
One of them recently scammed the heir of the Reeves family, a young man named Von Reeves, out of a substantial portion of his inheritance.
The scammer used my online alias to do it.
Specifically, he used my identity as Sir Streak."
Amelia’s brow tightened.
She was listening with the focused, calculating attention of a woman whose business instincts had just kicked in.
"I’ve been thinking about the right way to handle it," Stan continued.
"It’s not a problem I can solve through public confrontation, exposing one impersonator publicly just teaches the rest to be more careful.
What I need is a coordinated tracking operation.

Someone who can identify the scammers operating under my identity across multiple platforms and multiple geographies, and then make them pay in a way that sends a clear, lasting message to everyone else considering it."
He held her eye.
"You have Vanguard on retainer.
Vanguard has a serious intelligence and tracking division, I’ve been told as much, by people whose judgment I trust.
You also have the broader Warner Bros. network and your own connections beyond it.
Between Vanguard and your own resources, you have the ability to find these people and dismantle their operations in a way I can’t easily do on my own."
He let the proposition settle.
"Track them.
Identify the active impersonators.
Get the man who scammed Von Reeves first, that one is personal to me, and I want him made into a public example.
And after that, the rest.
Systematically.
Quietly.
Until the world understands that pretending to be Sir Streak is not something that goes unanswered."
He sat back slightly.
"That’s what I want.
If you genuinely want to repay me, that’s the help I’ll take."
Amelia did not respond immediately.
She held the cup in her hands and looked at him across the table with the careful, measured stillness of a woman processing an offer she had not been expecting.

The waiter set it down between them without comment and left.
Neither of them touched it.

chapters.title: Chapter 282: No Regrets
paragraphs: Amelia tilted her head slightly, the small, disbelieving smile still lingering on her face.
"Although, I have to admit, I’m a little surprised you’re Sir Streak. I knew you were popular. I just didn’t realize you were that popular."
"It’s a relatively recent development."

"Recent?" She raised an eyebrow. "Sir Streak has been the most discussed gifter on TikTuk Live for the past two weeks. I’ve heard your alias mentioned at media board meetings, Stan. You’re practically a phenomenon."
"It’s been an eventful two weeks."
"That is the understatement of the year."
She laughed softly, the first genuine laugh he had heard from her. Low, a little rough, the laugh of a woman whose throat had only recently relearned the motion after days of silence.
"Most people spend a decade building that kind of profile," she continued. "You managed it while studying at Peak University."
"It happened in stages."
"It happened in weeks."
Stan inclined his head, conceding the point.
Amelia took a sip of her coffee before setting the cup down again, shaking her head faintly.
"You’re an odd person, Stan Harrison."
"I’ve been told."
"In a good way. You keep doing things no one expects from you."
"Sometimes."
The answer drew another laugh from her, less guarded than the last.
From there, the conversation settled naturally into something easier.
Amelia asked about Ghost Signal, having seen several viral clips while recovering. Stan answered with the casual brevity he reserved for discussions of his own work.
She asked about the Wanhai Group next, carefully, professionally, the way one shareholder might question another about a position. He gave her enough to satisfy the question and nothing more.
Eventually, she asked about Sacha.
The topic surprised him.

The existence of his sister wasn’t exactly private information. Anyone willing to spend ten minutes researching Stan Harrison could discover that he had an older sister. Yet very few people ever bothered asking about her.
Stan found himself answering more openly.
Apart from Mia, Amelia was the first person in a very long time to ask about Sacha with genuine interest rather than casual curiosity.
Perhaps that shouldn’t have mattered. Yet somehow it did.
As he spoke, Amelia listened with an attentiveness that felt deeper than the conversation required.
She wasn’t merely hearing the words.
She was observing the way he spoke them.
The warmth that entered his voice whenever he mentioned his sister. The quiet protectiveness hidden beneath that warmth.
The complete absence of performance. This was not a man trying to appear caring. This was simply a man who loved his family.
’He’s very much unlike my father...’ she smiled...
And like many people who genuinely loved their family, he expressed it not through grand declarations, but through small, matter-of-fact details that slipped naturally into conversation.
Somewhere in the middle of listening to him, Amelia realized it was the strongest confirmation yet of what she had already concluded about his character.
Her gaze rested on him as he lifted his cup and took another sip of his flat white.
Without intending to, her eyes drifted lower.
To his lips. The realization struck almost immediately.
Her attention snapped upward. Their eyes met. A small jolt passed through her.
Because Stan had already been looking at her.
The eye contact lasted only a few seconds, but it felt longer. Long enough for warmth to begin climbing into her cheeks.
Long enough for her to become painfully aware of herself. Amelia broke the gaze first.
She turned her head slightly and looked toward the restaurant window with the careful composure of a woman who had just embarrassed herself in public and was determined not to acknowledge it.
Unfortunately, her blush proved far less cooperative. The faint pink remained. And deepened.
Stan noticed. Of course he noticed. But, as always, he was kind enough not to mention it.
He simply took another sip of his coffee. And allowed her dignity to survive the moment.
She drew a slow breath, gathered her courage, and turned back to him.
"Stan."
"Yes."
"I should get your Snapchat. So I can update you when we start identifying the impersonators.
She delivered it with crisp professionalism, framing the request as a practical necessity.
"I’ll give you mine too. That way you have a direct line."
"Sure."
The agreement came so easily that it nearly threw her off balance.
Before she could reconsider, she pulled out her phone, opened the QR scanner, and slid it across the table. Stan did the same. Their screens flashed almost simultaneously.
[Connection established: Stan] [Connection established: Amelia]
Amelia tapped into the newly added contact. His profile loaded.
The account name was exactly what she should have expected.
[Stan.]
No embellishments. No aliases. No clever usernames. Just Stan. She stared at it for a second.
Then the corner of her mouth twitched upward.
A small smile. One she immediately tried and failed to suppress. Her thumb drifted to the edit icon and the custom contact field opened.
Amelia glanced up. Stan was looking at his own phone.
’Good.’ She smiled and typed.
[My Hero ❤️]
The new label appeared beneath his profile picture. She stared at it. It was ridiculous.
Utterly, catastrophically ridiculous. This was the sort of contact name a teenage girl saved after developing her first serious crush.

It was not the sort of thing a twenty-eight-year-old Warner Bros. shareholder, responsible for multimillion-dollar decisions and accustomed to coordinating international business operations, should be doing.
Nor was it the sort of thing a woman who routinely directed armed security details should be doing.
The label remained on the screen. Amelia looked at it. Then she smiled. She loved it. She pressed Save. And had no regrets about it.
When she looked up again, a tiny trace of guilt still lingered in her expression, the look of someone who had just indulged herself and fully intended to keep the reason private.
Stan met her eyes. His expression carried a faint hint of amusement. Not because he knew what she had done. Because he clearly knew she had done something.
Fortunately, he was polite enough not to ask.
Amelia cleared her throat. Then she opened a conversation with him.

chapters.title: Chapter 283: Important to Her
paragraphs: Amelia cleared her throat. Then she opened a conversation with him. After several seconds of unnecessary consideration, she typed:
[Amelia: hi]
She stared at the message. Then she pressed send. The notification appeared.
[Delivered.]
Only then did the full reality of what she had done arrive.
She had just sent "hi" through Snapchat to a man sitting less than four feet away from her. At the same table. Drinking the same coffee. In the same conversation.
A wave of mild mortification swept through her.
’Am I doing too much?’ The thought arrived with startling clarity.
’He’s literally right there. Right there. And I’m messaging him on Snapchat.’
She considered delete it, but she ultimately decides against that. And determined not to expose herself, Amelia maintained a perfectly composed expression.
She turned toward the window. Picked up her coffee.
Was about to take a sip. But with so much in her mind and her heart, she carefully set the cup back down without actually drinking anything.
Across from her, Stan remained blissfully unaware of the crisis unfolding inside her head.
Or at least he appeared to be. Behind the embarrassment, however, another thought had begun quietly assembling itself.
A much more dangerous thought.
For two days since she awakened from coma, emotions had been accumulating inside her. Two days of warmth she couldn’t explain. Two days of having her understanding of people quietly rewritten.
Two days of catching herself staring at a photograph on her phone and smiling for reasons she preferred not to examine too closely.
And now the source of all of it sat directly across from her. Alone, relaxed. Close enough to reach across the table. No reporters. No assistants. No interruptions. No audience.
There might never be a better opportunity to tell him how she felt...
Amelia considered saying it. Not everything. Just enough.
’Stan, there’s something I want you to know.’
Or perhaps,
’I hope this doesn’t make things awkward, but...’
The words formed. Hovered in her mind and waited.
She imagined speaking them aloud. Then she imagined the consequences if she moved too quickly.
Stan had helped her.Saved her, in more ways than one. Refused repayment. Accepted her friendship.
Shown her a kindness so effortless that it somehow felt more meaningful than grand gestures ever could.
None of that meant he was ready for what she felt.
And if she pushed too hard. If she moved too fast. If she made him uncomfortable.
The possibility of him withdrawing from her, even slightly, produced a sharp, cold sensation beneath her ribs.
That feeling alone settled the matter.
’No I shouldn’t do that, Not today.’
She would tell him eventually. When the timing was right. When she understood her own feelings a little better.
When there was less risk of frightening away something she had only just begun to treasure.
But not today.
So Amelia said nothing but held her coffee and quietly enjoyed the simple fact that, for now, she had his number.
And he was still here.
Across the table, Stan’s phone emitted a soft notification. He glanced down.
A new Snapchat message sat at the top of the screen.
[Amelia: hi]
His gaze flicked briefly toward her.
From his angle, just before she turned her phone face-down, he caught the faintest glimpse of the custom name she’d saved for him.
[My Hero ❤️]
He registered it. The corner of his mouth twitched. For once, he decided not to tease her. Instead, he opened the chat and typed a reply.
[Stan: You’re not drinking your coffee. It’s going to go cold.]
He hit send. A second later, Amelia’s phone vibrated against the table.
She picked it up. Read the message.
And immediately felt warmth rush back into her cheeks.

She had, she realized, spent the last ten minutes alternately holding her coffee, setting it down, staring at Stan, thinking about Stan, and contemplating whether confessing her feelings to Stan would be an excellent decision or a catastrophic one.
Very little actual coffee consumption had occurred.
Amelia set the phone down. Picked up the cup. Took a deliberate sip. The coffee was, indeed, slightly cold.
She looked across the table at him smiled and lowered the cup. "Thank you."
"For what?"
"For saving my coffee."
"You weren’t drinking it."
"I had other things on my mind."
"Were they more important than coffee?"
Amelia met his eyes. For half a second, neither looked away.
"At the moment?" she said softly. "Yes."
Stan regarded her for a moment, faint suspicion mixing with amusement. Then one eyebrow lifted.
"I didn’t know you could tease."
The warmth returned to Amelia’s cheeks immediately. "Neither did I."
"I’ll have to adjust my assessment of you."
"Oh?"
"I had you categorized as extremely serious."
"I am extremely serious."
"Clearly."
The word carried just enough skepticism to make her laugh. A genuine laugh this time.
Amelia shook her head and took another sip of coffee.
"Perhaps not all the time."
"Good to know."
Something warm settled between them then, not quite flirting, not quite friendship, but no longer entirely either. Neither chose to examine it too closely.
A reluctant smile escaped her.
Unfortunately, that only made him look more amused.
The conversation drifted naturally after that.
The heavier subjects had already been dealt with, leaving only the comfortable, unstructured territory that existed between people who genuinely enjoyed each other’s company.
The fruit platter finally received some attention. The omelette arrived.
Stan attacked it with the focused efficiency of a man who had been awake since early morning and had only just remembered that food was necessary for continued operation.
Amelia watched him eat.
She didn’t comment. But every now and then that strange warmth inside her surfaced again, appearing as a small smile she never quite managed to suppress before it escaped.
Time passed easily. Eventually, the check arrived.
Amelia paid it before Stan could stop her. He made a token attempt to intervene.
She ignored him. He allowed her the victory.
A few minutes later, they stepped out into the late-morning sunlight.
Across the street, Emma and the Vanguard detail rose smoothly from their positions and reformed around Amelia at a respectful distance.
Stan noticed a subtle difference immediately that he didn’t notice a while back... The guards watched him differently now.
Back then when he saved Amelia, they had evaluated him as a potential threat.
Now they evaluated him as someone important to their client.
The distinction was slight. But unmistakable.

The omelette arrived.
Stan attacked it with the focused efficiency of a man who had been awake since early morning and had only just remembered that food was necessary for continued operation.
Amelia watched him eat.
She didn’t comment.
But every now and then that strange warmth inside her surfaced again, appearing as a small smile she never quite managed to suppress before it escaped.
Time passed easily.
Eventually, the check arrived.
Amelia paid it before Stan could stop her.
He made a token attempt to intervene.
She ignored him.
He allowed her the victory.
A few minutes later, they stepped out into the late-morning sunlight.
Across the street, Emma and the Vanguard detail rose smoothly from their positions and reformed around Amelia at a respectful distance.
Stan noticed a subtle difference immediately that he didn’t notice a while back...
The guards watched him differently now.
Back then when he saved Amelia, they had evaluated him as a potential threat.
Now they evaluated him as someone important to their client.
The distinction was slight.
But unmistakable.

chapters.title: Chapter 284: Upgrade Complete!
paragraphs: Together, Stan and Amelia crossed back toward the waiting convoy.
She stopped beside the rear door of the lead vehicle.
For a moment, neither of them spoke.
Amelia removed her sunglasses and hooked them onto the collar of her coat.
Her eyes met his. There was something there. Something she almost said.
Stan saw it. The hesitation. The impulse. The words that rose and then retreated. A heartbeat later, whatever it was disappeared behind her usual composure.
"I’ll start the operation immediately," she said quietly. "The moment we identify the people behind the impersonations, you’ll know."
"I know you will."
"And, Stan."
"Yes."
She drew a small breath. "Thank you."
His expression softened slightly. "For letting me help."
Her gaze dropped briefly before returning to his.
"Not just because of this situation. Because of everything."
She gestured vaguely, searching for words. "I needed somewhere to put what I’ve been carrying. You gave me that."
For a moment, neither spoke. Then Stan inclined his head. "You’re welcome."
The answer was simple. But somehow it felt sufficient.
Amelia held his gaze for another second. Then a small smile appeared.
Not quite shy. Not quite confident. Something in between. Something that belonged only to him.
She slid into the back seat and closed the door. The convoy pulled away moments later.
One vehicle after another merged into traffic and disappeared down the avenue.
Stan remained where he was. Watching. Only when the final vehicle vanished around the corner did he turn away.
His phone buzzed. He pulled it from his pocket.
A new Snapchat notification waited on the screen.
[Amelia: I’ll update you the moment we have anything.]
The contact name made him pause.
Then, despite himself, he smiled.
A small smile.
The sort that appeared only when nobody was around to see it.
He slipped the phone back into his pocket and headed toward Aurelia Heights.
The morning had delivered considerably more than he had expected when he woke up at Maya’s apartment.
A Vivian crisis.
A Wanhai meeting.
A private investment opportunity in Maya’s cosmetics venture.
A face-to-face meeting with Amelia.
A new operation targeting the Streak impersonators.
And a favorability counter that was somehow creeping toward one hundred and thirty on yet another bound target.
Not bad for a morning’s work.
By his watch, it still wasn’t noon.
He rode the elevator up to his floor and let himself into the apartment.
The familiar quiet settled around him.
For the first time all day, there was nothing demanding his attention.
No meetings. No crises. No decisions. Only silence.
In the corner of his vision, the system upgrade notification remained patiently waiting.
He ignored it. Whatever it brought would arrive soon enough.
For now, he dropped onto the couch and allowed himself a rare moment of simple satisfaction.
The world could wait a little longer. He had earned the quiet.
But Stan had barely crossed the threshold of his apartment when the notifications began arriving in rapid succession.
[Ding!]
[System upgrade complete.]
[New features unlocked: Points System Shop.]
[Ding!]
[Issuing pending rewards.]
[Reward for Sophie Youngs crossing favorability threshold 125: Divine Bronze Bone-Tempering Pill (×1).]
[Reward for Amelia Don crossing favorability threshold 125: Jade Purity Elixir (×1).]
Stan stopped in the middle of the entrance corridor.
For a moment, nothing happened.
Then faint light gathered above his palms. A shimmer formed in his left hand. Another in his right. The light condensed and solidified.
And abruptly became real.
In his left palm rested a small bronze-colored pill.

It was perfectly round, smooth to the touch, and faintly warm. The surface possessed a metallic sheen that seemed entirely inappropriate for medicine. Delicate patterns were etched across it, so fine they appeared almost woven into the material itself.
In his right hand sat a slender glass vial no taller than his thumb.
Inside swirled a clear jade-green liquid. The color was strange. Not bright. Not glowing. Yet somehow more vivid than any shade of green he had ever seen.
The liquid appeared to possess depth far beyond the confines of the tiny bottle, as though light was passing through layers that shouldn’t physically exist.
The stopper was sealed with the same intricate markings found on the pill.
Stan stared at both objects. Then at his hands. Then back at the objects.
Several seconds passed Finally, he exhaled.
"You have got to be kidding me."
The items felt real. Not visually real. Physically real. They possessed weight. Texture and temperature.
The pill pressed lightly against his skin. The glass bottle felt cool beneath his fingers. This was not augmented reality.
Not a hologram. Not another floating notification window. These things existed. And that was a problem.
Because the names attached to them were ridiculous.
’Divine Bronze Bone-Tempering Pill.’
’Jade Purity Elixir.’
The names sounded as though someone had stolen them directly from a cultivation novel.
Stan hads growing up to recognize the pattern instantly.
Bone tempering. Body refinement. Purification elixirs. Ancient medicines.
The sort of treasures old monsters fought over atop mist-covered mountains.
Not items that should be materializing in the hands of a university student standing in the entryway of an apartment building in modern Inksea.
For several moments, he simply stood there. Then his gaze narrowed slightly. The truly disturbing part wasn’t the items. The truly disturbing part was what they implied.
The system had already demonstrated abilities that violated every known law of reality.
Money appearing from nowhere. Until now, however, those miracles had remained largely invisible. Easy to mentally categorize as "system nonsense" and move on.

This was different. This was a physical object, not that he haven’t gotten something physical from the system, but this was completely unexpected, it wasn’t like the tea leaves reward he gained last time.
It was an impossible object. Something he thought always belonged to fiction and fiction alone.
Stan lowered his gaze to the bronze pill. "Are there really things about this world that aren’t public knowledge?"
His voice was quiet in the empty apartment. "Other people like me?"
His eyes shifted to the vial. "Other systems?"
A pause.
"Other things?"
The silence offered no answer. The system rarely explained itself.

chapters.title: Chapter 285: Beyond The Veil
paragraphs: Stan looked at the pill and the vial one final time before closing his hands around them.
The weight remained. Small, unmistakable and real.
Ever since receiving the system, such thoughts had crossed his mind more than once.
Yet now, more than ever, he couldn’t help but wonder whether the world was far stranger than he had ever imagined, and whether he had only just begun to glimpse its true nature.
Sighing, He walked into the living room, set them carefully on the kitchen counter, and pulled out his phone.
The system interface was already presenting him with the second new feature.
[Shop unlocked.]
[Available items: 1.]
He opened it.
A single product floated in his interface field.
[[Introduction to Earth.]
[Cost: 1 System Point]
Stan’s brow furrowed.
The title was generic. The book, if it was a book, was offered at the cost of a single system point. He had no system points currently on the balance. He was sitting at zero.
And yet,
He looked at the title again.

There was a quiet, instinctive pull toward it that he could not entirely explain. Introduction to Earth. The phrasing was deliberate. It was the kind of title you gave a book if you assumed the reader was approaching the planet from outside it. It was the kind of title a publisher would use if they expected their audience to be people who didn’t already know the basic facts.
It felt, in a way he couldn’t fully articulate, like exactly the document he was supposed to read in this exact moment of his life.
If there were superhumans on Earth, and the items on his counter strongly suggested there were, this book was likely to be where the answer to the question began.
He needed the point.
[Conversion rate available: Fiat currency (USD), 1 billion dollars : 1 system point.]
The notification arrived on cue.
Stan let out a slow, pained breath.
"Are you serious.
One billion dollars for a single system point.

It was, by any honest accounting, extortionate. The system had spent the past two weeks rewarding him with multi-billion-dollar windfalls and shareholdings, and now the moment he wanted to convert ordinary cash into something the system itself measured in, the exchange rate was set at a wall.
He turned the math over in his head.

He currently had, after the various transfers, the Wanhai purchases, the property gifts, and the Amelia treatment, roughly 1.6 billion dollars in liquid cash sitting in his primary account. A billion-dollar conversion would take a substantial chunk of that out in a single transfer.
But the question wasn’t really about cost.
The question was whether he wanted to know.

The pill and the bottle on his kitchen counter, in his honest reading of them, were a confirmation. The world he had grown up in was not the world he thought it was. There were systems of power he hadn’t been aware of. There were levels of existence he had been ignorant of. He had been walking around in a layer of reality that had quietly, deeply, never been the only layer.
He could continue not knowing. He could pocket the pill, drink the elixir, and let the rest of it remain mysterious.
Or he could buy the book.
The choice was, in the end, not really a choice.

He pulled up his phone’s banking interface, accessed his primary account, and mentally focused on the system at the same time. The instinct was clear, will the transaction, and the system would handle the rest.
He willed it.
One billion dollars vacated his account.

The deduction processed with the brisk efficiency of a wire transfer. His account balance shifted in real time. The number that appeared on his banking app was several hundred million dollars lower than it had been thirty seconds earlier.
A faint, distinctly uncomfortable pang moved through his chest as he watched the balance settle.
Losing a billion dollars in a single, instantaneous, intangible transaction was, even for him, even at this stage of his life felt uncomfortable.
But the system notification arrived a moment later.
[+1 System Point. Current balance: 1.]
He exhaled. Slowly. Through his teeth.
He tapped the Introduction to Earth in his shop interface.
[Purchase confirmed. Deducting 1 system point.]
[Item delivered.]
A weight materialized in his right hand.
He looked down. He was holding a book.
For a moment, that was all it appeared to be. No golden light..No mystical aura. No dramatic manifestation of cosmic power.
Just a book. A medium-sized hardback bound in dark navy cloth.
The cover was smooth beneath his fingers, the material matte and slightly textured. Centered on the front, pressed into the cover in clean silver lettering, were three words:
’Introduction to Earth.. huh’ Stan sighed and turned it over. The back cover was blank. No summary. No publisher. No barcode. No author photograph..Nothing.
The book carried none of the information normally attached to something intended for sale.
It existed solely as itself..He opened it..The first page contained only the title.
’Introduction to Earth.’
The second page contained a single additional line.
’A primer for those who have begun to see beyond the veil.’
Stan’s eyes lingered on the sentence. The apartment was silent. The words themselves were simple. Yet they carried a strange weight. Not because they were mysterious.
Because they were confirming something. The system was not treating him as someone who had discovered a secret.
It was treating him as someone who had finally become capable of noticing what had always been there.
Beyond the veil. Not a new world. The same world. Viewed differently.
Stan stared at the page for several seconds..Then he closed the book.
The soft thump of the cover sounded unusually loud in the quiet apartment.
He lowered himself onto one of the stools at the kitchen counter. The bronze pill sat a short distance away. The jade elixir rested beside it.
The book remained in his hands.

For a moment, he simply sat there. Reflecting. The morning replayed itself in fragments. Vivian’s crisis. The Wanhai meeting. Maya’s investment proposal. Breakfast with Amelia. The favorability rewards. The system upgrade.
By any reasonable standard, it had already been an absurdly eventful day.
And somehow none of it felt as significant as the object currently resting in his hands.
After all this was an explanation to his long list of questions, at least the beginning of one.
With a cultivation pill on his counter. An impossible elixir within arm’s reach.
And, at long last, something that looked suspiciously like answers.
Stan opened the book once more. Then he turned the page. And began to read.

chapters.title: Chapter 286: Pages Of A Lost Age
paragraphs: Stan turned to the second page. It marked the beginning of the first Chapter.
At the top of the page, printed in bold, imposing letters, were four words:
THE AGE OF DAO
Stan took note of the title and began to read;
Long before recorded history, Earth existed in an era later remembered as the Age of Dao.
The opening sentence carried an unusual weight, as though the text itself understood the significance of what it was revealing.
He continued.
The book described a world unlike anything modern humanity could imagine.
An Earth saturated with Qi.

Not the fictional energy of cultivation novels, but a real and measurable force that permeated every corner of the planet. Spirit veins coursed beneath continents like vast underground rivers. Sacred mountains birthed heavenly treasures. Ancient beasts roamed untamed wildernesses. Cultivation was not myth, religion, or legend. It was the foundation upon which civilization itself was built.
Yet humanity had not ruled that world.
According to the book, Earth had been shared by four great races:
Humans. Vampires. Werewolves. Demihumans.
Of the four, humanity had occupied the lowest position.
Humans possessed weak natural affinity for Qi. Their bodies were fragile, their lifespans short, and their senses dull compared to the supernatural races that shared the world with them.

The vampires had been born with extraordinary spiritual perception and an innate mastery over Blood Qi. Their bloodlines granted exceptional talent for cultivation, while the oldest among them routinely lived for centuries.
The werewolves were equally gifted.

Their physiques possessed a natural harmony with Earth and Beast Qi. Even young werewolves wielded strength capable of overwhelming ordinary humans. Their packs functioned as disciplined military societies, their hierarchies determined by power, lineage, and ancestral prestige.
The demihumans were the most diverse race of all.
Foxfolk. Catfolk. Serpentkin/Nagas. Hawkkin. Lionfolk. Rabbitfolk.

Countless bloodlines existed beneath the demihuman banner, each tracing its ancestry to ancient spiritual beasts. Their inherited gifts varied widely. Some possessed enhanced senses. Others wielded innate elemental abilities. Many enjoyed remarkable agility, resilience, or lifespans that stretched across centuries.
Yet beyond all these advantages, the supernatural races shared a far more terrifying trait.
Bloodlust Aura.
The book described it not as a psychological phenomenon but as a spiritual one.
A pressure carried within the soul itself.

To stand before a powerful vampire, werewolf, or demihuman was to feel every instinct screaming for survival. The weak found it difficult to breathe. Some collapsed under the pressure. Others fled. Many lost the will to fight before battle had even begun.
For thousands of years, humanity remained beneath the other races.
Entire human settlements existed as tributaries to vampire clans.
Others survived under the protection of werewolf packs.
Still others lived within territories governed by powerful demihuman houses.
To many among the supernatural races, ordinary humans were little different from livestock. Useful, intelligent, sometimes entertaining, but ultimately inferior.
Then everything began to change. The next section contained a single word.
Will
Stan unconsciously slowed his reading.
The book explained that, from time to time, a human would emerge whose spirit seemed completely immune to fear.
Men and women capable of standing before ancient vampire lords without lowering their heads.
Individuals whose determination transcended instinct itself.
Humans whose souls burned with such intensity that even supernatural predators found themselves unable to regard them as lesser beings.
These extraordinary individuals became known asTrue Humans.
The title had not originated among mankind.
It had been bestowed by the vampires, werewolves, and demihumans themselves.
To the supernatural races, a True Human represented humanity at its absolute pinnacle. A being who had overcome weakness through the sheer force of spirit. A person worthy of standing as an equal.
The appearance of every True Human became a major event.

Many rose to become legendary cultivators. Many founded sects whose names echoed through history. Many became rulers, sages, or conquerors. Some surpassed vampire monarchs, werewolf kings, and demihuman sovereigns alike in raw cultivation power.
Though their numbers remained few, their influence spread steadily across the world.
Humanity gradually ceased to be prey. Relations between the races began to evolve. Treaties were negotiated. Shared cities emerged. Trade flourished. Knowledge was exchanged.
Eventually, after centuries of cooperation and compromise, the four races forged a historic agreement known as the Fourfold Accord.
The pact endured for nearly three thousand years and prevented open war among the races.
The book referred to the era that followed as theGolden Age of Cultivation.
An age when immortals walked openly among mortals. An age when dragons still crossed the heavens. An age when sects hidden within cloud-wreathed mountains guided the course of nations.
An age when the greatest cultivators could cross oceans in a single step. An age when the four races stood united beneath Heaven.
Stan turned the page.
The Chapter ended with a single sentence.
’Then came the event that ended an era.’
A faint sense of foreboding settled in his chest. Without hesitation, he turned to the next Chapter.
THE NIGHT OF VANISHING
The next Chapter began with cold, meticulous precision.
’Without warning, the world changed.’
Stan continued reading.
According to the book, on a single night remembered only through fragmented records and scattered accounts, every vampire on Earth vanished.
Not their kings. Not their elders. Not merely the powerful. Every single one.

Entire kingdoms stood empty before dawn. Ancient bloodline clans disappeared without a trace. Cities inhabited exclusively by vampires became silent ghost cities overnight. Vast estates remained untouched. Treasuries remained sealed. Personal possessions lay exactly where their owners had left them.
Only the owners themselves were gone.
At the same time, the same night, the werewolves vanished as well.
Packs disappeared from forests. Tribes vanished from mountains. Fortified territories that had endured for millennia fell silent in a matter of hours.
From the greatest Alpha Kings to the youngest cubs, not a single werewolf remained anywhere on Earth.
The demihumans suffered the same fate. The great beast clans disappeared from sacred mountains. Ancient fox courts became deserted. Serpent/Naga kingdoms vanished.
The countless bloodlines that had once formed one of the world’s dominant races simply ceased to exist.
No survivors were recorded. No exceptions were found. Then came humanity’s loss.
Unlike the supernatural races, ordinary humans remained.
Farmers remained. Merchants remained. Soldiers remained. Kings remained. The weak remained. The untalented remained.
But every individual recognized as a True Human vanished. Every saint. Every legendary cultivator. Every founder of great sects.
Every human whose spirit and power had elevated them to stand as equals beside vampires, werewolves, and demihumans. Gone.
The disappearances occurred simultaneously across the entire planet.
No battles were recorded. No enemy was witnessed. No warning was given. Some vanished while meditating. Some vanished in the middle of conversations. Some disappeared while teaching disciples.
Others vanished while leading armies, presiding over courts, or traveling between sects.
Many left behind possessions. Most left behind nothing.
The event became known asThe Night of Vanishing.
No explanation was ever discovered.
Stan found himself slowing as he reached the end of the Chapter.
Then he read it again.
The detached tone of the text somehow made the account more unsettling.
There were no dramatic descriptions. No speculation. No attempts to exaggerate the tragedy.
The author simply presented the disappearances as historical fact.
Three great races had vanished from existence. Humanity’s strongest had vanished alongside them.
And the world had awakened the next morning to find an entire era missing.
The book offered no theories. No suspects. No answers. Only the event itself.
As if the disappearance of civilizations was as indisputable as the rising of the sun.
A strange chill settled over Stan’s spine.
By every instinct he possessed, the book did not feel like fiction. It felt like a record.
Slowly, he turned the page.

sentences.text: Stan turned to the second page.
It marked the beginning of the first Chapter.
At the top of the page, printed in bold, imposing letters, were four words:
THE AGE OF DAO
Stan took note of the title and began to read;
Long before recorded history, Earth existed in an era later remembered as the Age of Dao.
The opening sentence carried an unusual weight, as though the text itself understood the significance of what it was revealing.
He continued.
The book described a world unlike anything modern humanity could imagine.
An Earth saturated with Qi.
Not the fictional energy of cultivation novels, but a real and measurable force that permeated every corner of the planet.
Spirit veins coursed beneath continents like vast underground rivers.
Sacred mountains birthed heavenly treasures.
Ancient beasts roamed untamed wildernesses.
Cultivation was not myth, religion, or legend.
It was the foundation upon which civilization itself was built.
Yet humanity had not ruled that world.
According to the book, Earth had been shared by four great races:
Humans.
Vampires.
Werewolves.
Demihumans.
Of the four, humanity had occupied the lowest position.
Humans possessed weak natural affinity for Qi.
Their bodies were fragile, their lifespans short, and their senses dull compared to the supernatural races that shared the world with them.
The vampires had been born with extraordinary spiritual perception and an innate mastery over Blood Qi.
Their bloodlines granted exceptional talent for cultivation, while the oldest among them routinely lived for centuries.
The werewolves were equally gifted.
Their physiques possessed a natural harmony with Earth and Beast Qi.
Even young werewolves wielded strength capable of overwhelming ordinary humans.
Their packs functioned as disciplined military societies, their hierarchies determined by power, lineage, and ancestral prestige.
The demihumans were the most diverse race of all.
Foxfolk.
Catfolk.
Serpentkin/Nagas.
Hawkkin.
Lionfolk.
Rabbitfolk.
Countless bloodlines existed beneath the demihuman banner, each tracing its ancestry to ancient spiritual beasts.
Their inherited gifts varied widely.
Some possessed enhanced senses.
Others wielded innate elemental abilities.
Many enjoyed remarkable agility, resilience, or lifespans that stretched across centuries.
Yet beyond all these advantages, the supernatural races shared a far more terrifying trait.
Bloodlust Aura.
The book described it not as a psychological phenomenon but as a spiritual one.
A pressure carried within the soul itself.
To stand before a powerful vampire, werewolf, or demihuman was to feel every instinct screaming for survival.
The weak found it difficult to breathe.
Some collapsed under the pressure.
Others fled.
Many lost the will to fight before battle had even begun.
For thousands of years, humanity remained beneath the other races.
Entire human settlements existed as tributaries to vampire clans.
Others survived under the protection of werewolf packs.
Still others lived within territories governed by powerful demihuman houses.
To many among the supernatural races, ordinary humans were little different from livestock.
Useful, intelligent, sometimes entertaining, but ultimately inferior.
Then everything began to change.
The next section contained a single word.
Will
Stan unconsciously slowed his reading.
The book explained that, from time to time, a human would emerge whose spirit seemed completely immune to fear.
Men and women capable of standing before ancient vampire lords without lowering their heads.
Individuals whose determination transcended instinct itself.
Humans whose souls burned with such intensity that even supernatural predators found themselves unable to regard them as lesser beings.
These extraordinary individuals became known asTrue Humans.
The title had not originated among mankind.
It had been bestowed by the vampires, werewolves, and demihumans themselves.
To the supernatural races, a True Human represented humanity at its absolute pinnacle.
A being who had overcome weakness through the sheer force of spirit.
A person worthy of standing as an equal.
The appearance of every True Human became a major event.
Many rose to become legendary cultivators.
Many founded sects whose names echoed through history.
Many became rulers, sages, or conquerors.
Some surpassed vampire monarchs, werewolf kings, and demihuman sovereigns alike in raw cultivation power.
Though their numbers remained few, their influence spread steadily across the world.
Humanity gradually ceased to be prey.
Relations between the races began to evolve.
Treaties were negotiated.
Shared cities emerged.
Trade flourished.
Knowledge was exchanged.
Eventually, after centuries of cooperation and compromise, the four races forged a historic agreement known as the Fourfold Accord.
The pact endured for nearly three thousand years and prevented open war among the races.
The book referred to the era that followed as theGolden Age of Cultivation.
An age when immortals walked openly among mortals.
An age when dragons still crossed the heavens.
An age when sects hidden within cloud-wreathed mountains guided the course of nations.
An age when the greatest cultivators could cross oceans in a single step.
An age when the four races stood united beneath Heaven.

Treasuries remained sealed.

chapters.title: Chapter 287: The World That Was Forgotten
paragraphs: The next Chapter bore a simple title.
THE GREAT WITHERING
According to the book, the second great disaster arrived only a few years after theNight of Vanishing.
This time, it was not people who disappeared. It was the world itself that began to change. Qi, the invisible force upon which theAge of Daohad been built, started to fade.
The decline was gradual at first. Almost imperceptible. Yet it was undeniable. Spirit veins weakened. Sacred lands lost their vitality. Heavenly treasures became increasingly rare.
Regions that had once overflowed with spiritual energy slowly grew barren. Generation after generation, the decline accelerated.
Cultivators across the world noticed the change. Ancient clans launched investigations. Great sects gathered every record they possessed.
Powerful elders traveled between sacred lands in search of answers.
None were found. No source could be identified. No solution was discovered. No one understood why the very foundation of cultivation was disappearing.
As the centuries passed, cultivation became increasingly difficult.
Techniques that had once been commonplace became impossible.
Breakthroughs that had once required years now demanded decades. Entire cultivation paths vanished from existence.
The book preserved several theories proposed during that era.
Some believed the vanished races had served as anchors between Heaven and Earth, and that their disappearance had wounded the world’s spiritual foundation.
Others theorized that the vampires, werewolves, demihumans, and True Humans had somehow foreseen the catastrophe and chosen to leave before it arrived.
A few even suggested that this Qi Disappearance, calledthe Great Witheringwas merely the aftermath of whatever had caused the Night of Vanishing.
None of these theories were ever proven.
In the end, most surviving cultivators arrived at the same conclusion. A conclusion born not from understanding, but from fear.
Whatever force had removed entire races from existence in a single night remained beyond comprehension.
And if it had been capable of erasing the vampires, the werewolves, the demihumans, and every True Human on Earth simultaneously...
Then no one remaining possessed the power to oppose it. Fear spread throughout the cultivation world. Not the fear of defeat. Not the fear of death. But the fear of something unknown.
Something vast enough to erase civilizations without resistance. Something so incomprehensible that even the greatest cultivators could not explain it.
In response, the surviving sects withdrew from public life.
The book described the beginning of what later generations would call the Hidden World.
It was not a single event, but a process that unfolded over centuries.
One by one, the remaining cultivators either went into seclusion, deep sleep to preserve life span and like that cultivators were erased from history. Existing only in fictional stories.
Records were destroyed. Artifacts were concealed. Ancient libraries vanished. Memories were altered. Witnesses were silenced. Knowledge was buried.

Cultivation techniques written in the ancient Dao language gradually became incomprehensible to ordinary humans, and the few cultivators who still understood those texts took deliberate steps to ensure they would not survive into the modern age.
The world forgot. And as the world forgot, humanity inherited the Earth.
Without sufficient Qi, cultivation became nearly impossible.
The existence of vampires, werewolves, demihumans, spirit beasts, and immortals slowly transformed into myths.

The Age of Dao faded into legend. The Golden Age became folklore. The Great Withering became a mystery. And the Night of Vanishing became a secret so unsettling that even hidden cultivators refused to discuss it.
By the modern era, only a handful of ancient organizations still remembered fragments of the truth..Even they possessed little more than fragments. Broken records. Half-preserved traditions.
Scattered accounts passed down through generations. Because the greatest mystery of all remained unsolved.
Where did the Qi go?
Where did the vampires go?
Where did the werewolves go?
Where did the demihumans go?
Where did the True Humans go?
The book paused there. Then came the another passage of the Chapter.
A passage preserved from some of the oldest surviving records in existence.
And according to the book, every surviving source agreed upon one terrifying fact.
The Night of Vanishing was not a war. It was not a plague. It was not a natural disaster. It was not an extinction. Done by someone who had probably broken to the peak of cultivation and beyond.
Stan’s eyes lingered on the next line. A faint chill crawled up his spine.
The words seemed strangely out of place among the otherwise scholarly text.
As though they had been copied directly from a witness who had seen the impossible.
’Something called them. Probably.’
For several seconds, Stan simply stared. Then he read the final sentence.
’And they went.’
Silence filled the room. Stan slowly closed his eyes. The words lingered in his mind long after he had finished reading them.
Not because they answered anything. But because they raised a question far more unsettling than extinction.

If they had been destroyed, there would have been remains. If they had been defeated, there would have been a victor. If they had perished, there would have been evidence. But that was not what the records claimed.
The records claimed they had been called. And that they had answered.
After a long moment, Stan opened his eyes once more.
Then he turned the page and continued reading.
THE FORGETTING
The next Chapter described the long, gradual erasure that followed the Great Withering. It had not been a single event. It had been a process.
A process that unfolded across centuries, generation after generation, until the original truth had been buried beneath the accumulated weight of ordinary history.
The surviving sects, according to the book, eventually came to believe that preserving too much knowledge of the old world was dangerous.
Whether that belief had been wisdom or paranoia remained a matter of debate even within the hidden world.
The book offered no definitive judgment. It merely recorded the consequences.
Over time, the remaining cultivators initiated what later historians of the hidden world would callThe Forgetting.
It became one of the largest coordinated efforts to erase knowledge in human history.
Ancient records were hidden. Others were destroyed. Libraries vanished. Historical accounts were removed from circulation. Artifacts disappeared into sealed vaults.
The ruins of supernatural civilizations were quietly demolished, buried, or concealed beneath ordinary structures.
Evidence of vampires, werewolves, demihumans, spirit beasts, and cultivators was systematically removed from the public record.
The process was neither rapid nor absolute. It unfolded over centuries. Each generation inherited less knowledge than the one before it.
Stories became legends. Legends became myths. Myths became fairy tales.
And eventually, even theAge of Daoitself faded from public memory.
To modern humanity, the book stated plainly, vampires, werewolves, demihumans, and cultivators had become creatures of fiction.
Schools taught no history of them. Universities possessed no accepted evidence of them.
Mainstream historians dismissed them as products of folklore, imagination, and cultural storytelling.
To the overwhelming majority of humanity, the supernatural races had never existed at all.
Then came a line set apart from the rest of the text.
’Yet the truth never disappeared completely.’
Stan found himself reading more slowly. The book lingered on the point. Fragments had survived.
Ancient memories had persisted in unexpected places. Folktales passed from grandparents to grandchildren. Regional legends preserving distorted accounts of genuine events.
Symbols from vanished civilizations appearing in artwork whose creators no longer understood their meaning.
Stories emerging independently across distant cultures despite having no obvious connection.
Again and again, traces of the old world resurfaced. Never whole. Never accurate. Yet never entirely gone.
The hidden world found the phenomenon both fascinating and unsettling.
Humanity had forgotten. Yet somewhere deep within its collective memory, it still remembered.
The surviving cultivators eventually developed a theory to explain the phenomenon.
They called itAncestral Echoes.

According to the theory, traces of the old world still existed within humanity itself. The Age of Dao had endured for thousands of years. During that vast span of time, bloodlines had intertwined countless times.
The descendants of cultivators, vampires, werewolves, and demihumans had gradually merged into the greater human population.
Though their inheritances had long since become dormant, something remained. Not power. Not cultivation but memory. Or perhaps the faint shadow of memory.
Occasionally those buried remnants surfaced. A dream that felt impossibly vivid. An intuition with no clear source. A story idea that appeared fully formed.
A fictional world that felt strangely familiar.
A sense of recognition when encountering something that should have been entirely imaginary.
Most people called such things creativity. The hidden world called them remembrance. The book’s tone shifted subtly at this point. Not enough to become informal.
Just enough for Stan to sense the faintest trace of irony beneath the author’s words.
And so, after centuries of concealment, the truth survived.
Not in official histories. Not in archaeological records. Not in scholarly institutions. But in stories. In novels. In films. In games. In folklore.
In the collective imagination of a species that no longer remembered why it remembered.
Modern humanity laughs at tales of vampires, werewolves, beastfolk, immortals, and cultivation.
Never realizing that many of those stories are distorted reflections of a world that once existed.
A world that lived beneath the same sky.
A world that vanished during theNight of Vanishing.
A world whose echoes still linger in the dreams of its descendants.
The final line stood alone;
’And a world that some fear may one day return’
Stan read the passage twice. Then a third time. His thoughts drifted.
He remembered the cultivation novels he had devoured as a teenager.
The vampire dramas that had dominated entire years of popular culture.
The endless stream of werewolf stories, beastfolk fantasies, supernatural romances, urban legends, and fantasy worlds that humanity seemed endlessly fascinated by.
An odd realization settled over him.
The book was claiming that modern imagination was not creating those stories from nothing.
It was remembering them. Poorly and imperfectly.
Through layers of distortion accumulated across centuries. But remembering them nonetheless. He found himself thinking about how strangely compelling such stories had always felt.
As though some part of humanity instinctively recognized them.
As though the world had forgotten something important and had spent generations trying to reconstruct it through fiction.
The thought settled heavily in his chest. Not frightening. Not comforting. Simply weighty.
Like a truth too large to fully grasp. For several moments, Stan sat in silence.
Then he turned the page.
