chapters.title: Chapter 288: The Last Lesson
paragraphs: The final Chapter opened with humanity standing alone.
The vampires were gone. The werewolves were gone. The demihumans were gone. TheTrue Humanswere gone.
For the first time since the beginning of recorded history, ordinary mankind stood as the sole dominant race upon Earth.
Yet according to the book, humanity’s first emotion had not been triumph.
It had been fear. The vanished races had not been defeated. They had not been conquered. They had not been exterminated. No great war had been won. No final battle had been fought.
No victorious banner had been raised over fallen enemies.
The vampires had simply disappeared. The werewolves had simply disappeared. The demihumans had simply disappeared.
And the strongest among humanity had disappeared alongside them.
That distinction mattered. Because what had been defeated could remain defeated. But what had vanished could return.
Fragments of ancient records survived from the centuries immediately following theNight of Vanishing.
Though incomplete, they preserved one uncomfortable truth.
The surviving cultivators never believed the supernatural races were truly gone forever. Only absent. And absence, unlike death, could end.

Many among the hidden world feared that if the vampires, werewolves, and demihumans ever returned while humanity remained weak, the balance of power that had governed theAge of Daowould reassert itself.
Humanity would once again find itself at the bottom of the hierarchy.
As Qi continued to fade and cultivation became increasingly impossible, mankind searched for another path.
Unable to master Heaven, humanity turned toward mastering the world itself.
Thus began theAge of Progress.

The book described the rise of modern civilization from a perspective Stan had never encountered before. Technology advanced at a pace unprecedented in human history. Kingdoms became nations. Nations became industrial powers. Industry gave birth to science. Science gave birth to machines.
Machines gave birth to a civilization whose scale would have seemed impossible during the Age of Dao.

Human populations exploded. Cities spread across continents. Roads connected nations. Railways reshaped economies. Ships conquered oceans. Aircraft conquered the skies. Satellites conquered near-Earth space.
Humanity multiplied into the billions and extended its reach into nearly every corner of the planet.
Yet the book argued that this transformation was not entirely what modern historians believed it to be.
A passage near the center of the Chapter was emphasized.
Many later historians would claim that modern civilization was born from ambition.
The surviving records suggest otherwise.
It was born from fear.
Stan found himself reading more slowly.

Fear that the vampires might return. Fear that the werewolves might emerge once more. Fear that the demihuman clans might reclaim the world they once shared. Fear that humanity would again stand powerless before forces it could not match.
The book did not claim that ordinary people understood this fear. Most did not. Most never learned the truth.
But institutions remembered. Great Families with history that went way back remembered. The hidden world remembered. And memory shaped decisions.
Across the centuries, technology became humanity’s answer to cultivation. Its substitute, its shield and its weapon.
The more Stan read, the stranger the perspective became. He thought about every military breakthrough in modern history.
Every classified weapons program. Every technological race between rival nations. Every massive infrastructure project.
The industrial revolution. The arms race. The nuclear age. The space race. The information age. The relentless acceleration of civilization itself.
The book’s interpretation cast all of it in a different light. Less like the natural ambition of an advancing species. And more like the behavior of a survivor preparing for a future threat.
A civilization building defenses against an enemy it could not be certain was gone.
For the first time, Stan found himself wondering whether humanity’s greatest achievement was not progress itself, but preparation.
He eventually reached the final page of the Chapter.
Only a single passage remained. It occupied the center of the page. Nothing else accompanied it.
No explanation. No footnotes. No elaboration. Just a final observation.
’Yet despite humanity’s achievements, one place remained largely untouched.’
Stan frowned slightly. He continued reading.
’One continent remained isolated.’
’One continent remained unexplained.’
’Despite it’s technology one continent was hard for humanity’s approach’
A strange feeling stirred in the back of his mind. Then came the final sentence.
’That place was later calledAntarctica.’
Stan stopped. For several seconds, he simply stared at the page.
The Chapter ended there. No explanation followed. No context. No answers. Just a name.
A single frozen continent sitting at the bottom of the world.
Yet somehow, after everything he had just read, the mention of Antarctica felt less like geography and more like a warning.
He read the line again. He read it a third time.
Then he closed the book slowly and set it down on the kitchen counter beside the elixir and the pill.
’Antarctica.’

He stared at the cover of the book, Introduction to Earth, a plain navy hardback with no author listed, and felt the small, unmistakable click of a pattern locking into place somewhere at the back of his mind.
The book had been compiled by the system. Of that, he was now certain.

Everything about its language, its structure, its careful selection of information, its abrupt ending, all of it pointed toward the same conclusion. This was not a work of independent scholarship. It was a curated primer. The system had chosen exactly what to include and exactly how much to reveal.
And it had ended the book on Antarctica. The implication was not subtle. The system was pointing him there.

Whatever lay in Antarctica, whatever the book had implied with that single, deliberately unfinished sentence, was the next thing he was supposed to investigate. Or, at the very least, the next thing he was supposed to know about.

He thought about the modern public understanding of Antarctica. The official narrative. The international treaty system that designated the continent as a scientific preserve. The scattered research stations buried across the ice.

He thought about the strange persistence with which Antarctica appeared in conspiracy theories of every variety, ancient cities, hidden bases, secret programs, unexplained anomalies, restricted zones.
He thought about how easily he had dismissed those stories in the past. And he thought about how differently they sat with him now.
’Was there something hidden in Antarctica?’
He had more questions than answers.

The book had given him only the shape of the question, not its solution. He had half expected that once he finished reading, everything would click into place. Instead, all he had gained were even more mysteries.
Yet for the first time since the system had activated two weeks ago, Stan Harrison felt that he was beginning to understand, in broad strokes, in dim outline, what he had actually been pulled into.
He was not simply the beneficiary of a wealth-generating system. He was not an unusual young man who had been handed money and strength by a benevolent voice in his head.
He was a participant in something far larger than that.
Something that, according to the book in front of him, had been quietly shaping the world for thousands of years.
He sat at the kitchen counter for a long moment.

The bronze pill caught the morning sunlight streaming through the window. The jade elixir glimmered faintly within its small glass bottle. The book lay closed beside them, its navy cover blank and patient.
The morning had begun with him leaving Maya and Sophie after having breakfast with them, then breakfast with Amelia.
Now It was ending with the realization that he was no longer living in the world he had thought he was living in.
He let out a slow breath.
"Antarctica."
He spoke the word quietly to the empty apartment. It did not feel like a destination yet. It felt like a thread. But for now, the thread was enough.
He picked up the pill in his right hand and the bottle in his left.
The book had told him what kind of world he was living in. It had not told him how to use the tools the system had given him.
Fortunately, that part seemed straightforward.

The descriptions of both treasures had been clear. More importantly, the system had done nothing but help him since its arrival. It had given him opportunities, resources, and knowledge that had already transformed his life.
There was always risk in the unknown. But this did not feel reckless. It felt like the next step.
Stan studied the bronze pill for a moment longer, then glanced at the jade elixir.
Whatever happened next, he suspected there would be no turning back afterward.

chapters.title: Chapter 289: The Price Of Bronze
paragraphs: Stan took a deep, deliberate breath.

The Divine Bronze Bone-Tempering Pill sat in his right palm, dark and warm and slightly heavier than it should have been for its size. He turned it over once between his thumb and forefinger, studying the faint, almost invisible script etched across its surface.
He set the jade elixir aside for now. The bottle could wait. Whatever it did, he wanted to take the pill first.
He weighed it once more, exhaled, and brought it to his mouth.

Though he didn’t let it linger on his tongue, the instant the pill touched its tip, a sharp, electric sting spread across his taste buds. It wasn’t the fiery burn of spice or the harsh bite of alcohol, but something far stranger, more invasive. It felt as though the inside of his mouth had been brushed by a low-voltage current, every nerve ending simultaneously numbed and set ablaze.
He swallowed almost immediately, more out of instinct than intention.
A wave of intense heat followed the pill down his throat.

It was, in the first half-second, comparable to drinking a long, deep gulp of high-proof whiskey. The kind of swallow that burned all the way down. The kind that left a hot, glowing line behind it as it traveled.
In the second half-second, the comparison stopped working.
The heat intensified with terrifying speed, becoming several orders of magnitude harsher than any alcohol he had ever tasted. It no longer felt like a chemical burn. It felt alive.

The scorching sensation seemed to crawl deliberately through his throat, spreading itself across every inch it touched, as though it were searching for every exposed nerve. It left behind not mere warmth, but a trail of nerves screaming in protest, each one flaring with a fierce, almost sentient agony that made his muscles tense involuntarily.
The pill reached his stomach and it dissolved instantly. And then it stopped behaving like medicine altogether.
Stan staggered.

A wave of unbearable heat erupted from deep within his abdomen, exploding through his body with such violence that the edges of his vision flashed white. The pill’s effects ignored every law of biology he understood. It did not seep into his bloodstream or spread through his circulatory system. It propagated through him instantaneously, as though every nerve in his body had been waiting for a signal, and that signal had finally arrived.
Then he felt his bones.
That was what he would remember most vividly afterward, not the heat, not the paralysis, but the impossible awareness that he could feel his own skeleton.
His femurs. His tibias. The bones of his arms. His ribs. His spine. His skull.
Every bone in his body had been brought into perfect, horrifying focus, as though flesh, muscle, and skin had ceased to exist, leaving only his skeleton illuminated within him.
And every single bone was burning. It felt as though molten bronze had been poured directly into the marrow of every bone he possessed.
A ragged, involuntary cry ripped from his throat as his legs buckled beneath him.

He slammed into the kitchen counter, barely catching himself before he hit the floor. His fingers dug into the countertop until his knuckles whitened, using it to force himself upright one final time. Already, his body was beginning to betray him.
His vision tunneled.
A metallic taste flooded his mouth, blood, saliva, or perhaps both.
His knees refused to lock. Violent tremors seized his shoulders, not from cold, but from a nervous system overwhelmed by a heat it had no capacity to endure.
’Bed. Bed!’
The thought surfaced through the rapidly shrinking window of his consciousness.
He had seconds. Perhaps four. Perhaps five. Before the paralysis consuming his body became absolute.
Grinding his teeth against the agony, Stan gathered every shred of will he possessed and forced himself forward.
Three stumbling steps. Four more. Then six, each one clumsier than the last, until walking became controlled falling.
He reached the bedroom doorway just as his legs finally gave out.
His body pitched forward and he struck the mattress like a felled tree.
Everything stopped. He couldn’t move. He couldn’t even shift his weight. His arms had locked rigid at his sides. His legs refused the slightest command.
Half his face was buried in the pillow, his neck twisted at an awkward angle that should have been agonizing on its own, yet it barely registered.
The paralysis was complete. Whatever control had carried him from the kitchen to the bedroom had been the last reserve his body could offer.
Then the true agony began.
The burning in his bones intensified.
Some distant, detached part of Stan’s mind, the part still capable of coherent thought, understood what was happening.
The pill was doing exactly what its name promised; Bone-tempering.

It was rewriting the very architecture of his skeleton at a level so fundamental that his nervous system possessed no language for the experience. This wasn’t ordinary pain. Ordinary pain was the body’s warning that something had been injured.
This was different; this was the body trying to comprehend the impossible.
His bones were being dismantled and rebuilt simultaneously, and every nerve anchored to them was faithfully transmitting the process to his brain without mercy or restraint.
Stan groaned through clenched teeth.
Sweat poured from him in torrents. His shirt was already soaked through, clinging to his skin. Beneath him, the bedsheet darkened as moisture spread across the fabric.
His entire body felt impossibly hot.

Heat radiated from his skin in relentless waves. Cool air brushed against the sweat coating his arms and neck, only for fresh perspiration to replace what had already begun to evaporate. It felt as though his body had become a furnace, burning from the inside out.
Then another wave struck.
His bones felt as though they were breaking.
Not all at once. One after another; His femurs, his ribs, his jaw, his spine, his forearms, his hips.

The agony rolled through him like seismic aftershocks, each surge igniting a fresh explosion of pain before fading just enough for the next to arrive. There was never relief, only brief valleys between impossible peaks.
’Fuck!’
The thought flashed through his mind with the simple, crystalline clarity that only unbearable pain could produce.
’Fuck!’
’Fuck!!’
’Fuck!!!’
He had read about this countless times in cultivation novels.
From the safety of a reader’s perspective, he had always assumed the authors were embellishing.
The protagonists screaming until their voices gave out. The cultivators writhing across stone floors during body-tempering.
The prodigies biting through their own tongues to keep from crying out during breakthroughs.
He had read those scenes with detached amusement, convinced that the suffering was exaggerated for dramatic effect.
He even remembered dismissing one particular protagonist as a wimp for screaming through an almost identical tempering sequence.
A distant, almost hysterical laugh echoed somewhere in the back of his mind.
He took it back. He took it all back. If anything, those authors had been restrained.
No words on a page could truly convey what it felt like to have every bone in your body remade while remaining painfully conscious throughout the process.
This, What was happening to him now, on his bed in Aurelia Heights, on an otherwise ordinary afternoon in Inksea, This was the reality behind those stories.
"Fuck..." he croaked aloud.
The word scraped past teeth that refused to unclench.
"Fuck..."
His vision had become a watery blur. Tears streamed unchecked down his face, but they carried no emotion. They weren’t born of fear or despair.
His body was simply reacting.
His eyes watered for the same reason sweat drenched his skin: the pill’s transformation was reaching every part of him.
He could feel it working through the tiny bones of his inner ears.
Through the delicate structures surrounding his eyes.
Through the bones of his hands, wrists, feet, and fingers.
Every dense, calcified structure in his body had become another battlefield in the relentless process of tempering.
He couldn’t tell how much of the pill’s power was being spent on his bones and how much was spilling into the rest of his body.
From the inside, it felt like all of it.

Yet some detached corner of his mind, the part still capable of reason, understood that couldn’t be true. The pill was called the Divine Bronze Bone-Tempering Pill for a reason. Most of its power had to be focused on his skeleton. The heat coursing through his organs, the pressure behind his eyes, the burning beneath his skin... those were only secondary effects, the excess energy radiating outward from the true transformation.
Perhaps ninety percent of the pill’s power was devoted to his bones.
The remaining ten percent was enough to make every other part of his body feel as though it were being forged alongside them.
If ten percent felt like this... It’s hard to imagine what ninety percent was doing to his femurs.
His consciousness began to slip.

The temptation was overwhelming. The human mind wasn’t built to remain awake through prolonged agony. Faced with pain beyond its ability to process, it sought escape. Darkness crept in at the edges of his awareness, soft and inviting.
’Just close your eyes.’
’Just let go.’
’You’ll wake up when it’s over.’
For one dangerous moment, the offer sounded almost irresistible.
Then something inside him rejected it. Not with logic but with instinct.
A deep, primal refusal rose from somewhere beyond conscious thought.
’No!’
He couldn’t have explained why, even to himself.
Perhaps it was stubbornness. A refusal to become nothing more than a passive subject while the System remade his body.
Perhaps it was the nagging certainty that something important was happening, something he needed to witness rather than awaken to after the fact. Or perhaps it was something older.
He had lived through enough as a teenager to learn one lesson that pain had carved into him:
When life became unbearable, the answer wasn’t to surrender consciousness and hope the world would still be waiting when you returned.
So he refused. He held on.
His jaw remained clenched so tightly that it ached.
Sweat streamed from every pore. Every muscle trembled uncontrollably. His body begged for oblivion. His mind denied it.
And so Stan endured.

The temptation was overwhelming.
The human mind wasn’t built to remain awake through prolonged agony.
Faced with pain beyond its ability to process, it sought escape.
Darkness crept in at the edges of his awareness, soft and inviting.
’Just close your eyes.’
’Just let go.’
’You’ll wake up when it’s over.’
For one dangerous moment, the offer sounded almost irresistible.
Then something inside him rejected it.
Not with logic but with instinct.
A deep, primal refusal rose from somewhere beyond conscious thought.
’No!’
He couldn’t have explained why, even to himself.
Perhaps it was stubbornness.
A refusal to become nothing more than a passive subject while the System remade his body.
Perhaps it was the nagging certainty that something important was happening, something he needed to witness rather than awaken to after the fact.
Or perhaps it was something older.
He had lived through enough as a teenager to learn one lesson that pain had carved into him:
When life became unbearable, the answer wasn’t to surrender consciousness and hope the world would still be waiting when you returned.
So he refused.
He held on.
His jaw remained clenched so tightly that it ached.
Sweat streamed from every pore.
Every muscle trembled uncontrollably.
His body begged for oblivion.
His mind denied it.
And so Stan endured.

chapters.title: Chapter 290: Reforged
paragraphs: Time ceased to have meaning.
The pain came in relentless waves. They rose, crashed and receded. Only to gather strength and break over him again.
The intervals between them became the only measure of time he possessed, and even those dissolved into something meaningless. Minutes and seconds no longer existed. There was only the next wave.
More than once, he convinced himself the worst had finally passed.
He was wrong. Every time, every single time.
At one point, he became certain he was dying. Sometime later, he wasn’t entirely sure dying would be worse than enduring another wave.
Then, through the haze of agony, another thought surfaced.
’Sacha.’
What would happen if she came home and found him like this?
The image cut through the pain with startling clarity, anchoring him just enough to keep his mind from slipping away.
Other faces followed.
’Sophie.’
’Maya.’
’Mia.’
’Amelia.’
’Sarah.’
They didn’t come as memories or conversations, only fleeting impressions, faces he wanted to see again, people he refused to leave behind.
Each became another reason to endure. So he endured. Gradually...
Almost imperceptibly at first... The waves began to weaken. The intervals stretched longer.
The peaks lost their impossible height.
The fire consuming his skeleton eased from molten agony to blistering heat.
From blistering heat to a deep, lingering warmth.
Then to the strange, exhausted ache of a body that had survived something it had never been meant to experience.
His fingers twitched. For a moment, the movement confused him. He had forgotten he even had fingers.
A breath later, feeling returned to his right arm. Then his left. His neck. His jaw.
The paralysis loosened its grip piece by piece until, with immense effort, he managed to turn his head a fraction against the pillow.
The movement was almost laughably small.
Yet in that moment, it felt like the greatest victory of his life. The pain... Was gone.
’Finally’ he sighed as he lay motionless, drenched in sweat, drawing slow, careful breaths as his body gradually accepted that the torment had finally ended.
Silence settled over the room. Then he noticed something else.
Energy. It flowed through him in a quiet, unhurried current. Not the violent, crackling force of the pill reshaping his body.
This was different. Gentle. Steady.
Like a calm river winding through every corner of his being.
He felt it in his arms. His legs. His chest. Along the length of his spine.
And most distinctly, gathering in slow, rhythmic currents within his lower abdomen.
Yet... Something wasn’t right.
The energy flowed effortlessly through his body, nourishing every limb, every muscle, every bone that had just been reforged.
But whenever it reached his lower abdomen, it seemed to... hesitate. As though it had arrived before a sealed gate. It gathered there, pressing gently against an invisible barrier.
Searching. Waiting. Unable to move any farther.
A strange sense of blockage settled over him. Not painful, but uncomfortable and incomplete.
Like a river that had found its destination, only to discover the entrance sealed shut.
Stan let out a long, slow breath.
Then he sat up. The motion was effortless. Far too effortless.
His body felt... new. Not larger. Not visibly stronger.
Simply new, as though every joint, muscle, tendon, and bone had been quietly dismantled, refined, and rebuilt while he had endured the storm.
He slowly clenched his right hand into a fist. It closed with perfect precision.
As he stared at it, he became aware of something he had never experienced before.
He could feel his bones. Not pain nor discomfort, Just pure awareness.
A quiet, instinctive understanding of the framework beneath his flesh, the way a master swordsman understood the balance of his blade without needing to think about it.
His skeleton no longer felt like something hidden inside him.
It felt like an extension of his consciousness.
He flexed his fingers. Rotated his wrist. Rolled his shoulders. Turned his neck from side to side.
Every movement carried the same unmistakable impression.
Strength.
Not swollen muscles or explosive power. Structural strength. The kind that began with the skeleton itself. He couldn’t see any visible difference.
Yet his body knew. His bones had become denser. Harder. More resilient.
If he had to estimate, they were now roughly five times stronger than they had been only three hours earlier.
"What..." he murmured, staring at his hand.
"What is this power?" His gaze drifted toward his abdomen. "And what is this energy I’m feeling?
His thoughts returned to the ancient book. More specifically... The words Qi.
He quietly tested the word. "Qi."
The moment it left his lips, it felt... correct.
As though his body recognized the name before his mind did. He stood there in silence. If the current flowing through him truly was Qi...
If the Divine Bronze Bone-Tempering Pill had done more than strengthen his skeleton, if it had awakened within him the very energy the ancient text claimed had all but disappeared from Earth...
Then he possessed something that almost no one alive in the modern world should have. The implications were staggering.
He deliberately pushed them aside. There would be time to investigate later.
For now... He swung his legs over the edge of the bed and stood.
His balance was flawless. No lingering weakness. No soreness. No stiffness.
It was as though his body had forgotten it had spent three hours being torn apart and reforged.
His eyes drifted to the clock on the bedside table. He froze. His brows slowly lifted.
He had swallowed the pill at roughly eleven fifteen that morning.
The digital clock now displayed 2:30 PM.
Three hours.
"...Damn." He exhaled a quiet laugh, shaking his head. "It’s been three hours."
The number felt absurd. Inside the experience, it had stretched into what felt like days.
Outside it... It had occupied only a single afternoon. A quiet respect for himself surfaced.
He had remained conscious through three uninterrupted hours of body-rewriting agony.
No blackouts. No surrender. He had endured every second. Perhaps his tolerance for pain had always been greater than he’d believed.
Or perhaps sheer stubbornness had carried him where endurance alone could not.
His gaze shifted to the bed. The bedsheets were soaked.
Dark patches of sweat marked nearly every inch where his body had lain, with faint white traces of drying salt already beginning to appear where the moisture had evaporated.
The pillow was no better.
The room carried the faint metallic scent of a body pushed far beyond ordinary physical limits.
Stan sighed. ’Well... That’s going to need washing.’
He stripped the bedding off in one smooth motion, bundled it under one arm, and carried it to the laundry room.
After loading the washing machine, he selected the longest hot-water cycle before returning to his bedroom.
His clothes were no better than the sheets. Sweat clung to every thread.
He peeled them off, dropped them into a second laundry basket, then picked up the jade vial from where he had left it.
With the Jade Purity Elixir resting in his hand, he walked toward the bathroom.
Whatever came next... He had a feeling it wasn’t going to be as simple as taking a shower.

chapters.title: Chapter 291: Purification
paragraphs: The elixir bottle was small. Stan turned it over slowly beneath the bathroom light.

The pale jade liquid within the glass glowed with a soft, muted radiance. It wasn’t bright enough to illuminate the room, yet neither did it seem to be reflecting the overhead light. The glow appeared to come from the liquid itself, subtle and self-contained.
He studied it for another moment before letting out a quiet breath.
"It’s called a Purity Elixir," he muttered. "And elixirs are supposed to be... gentler than pills."
He paused. "...Right?"
Silence. The bathroom, unsurprisingly, offered no opinion. Stan gave a small, resigned nod.
"Yeah. That’s about the level of guidance I’ve been getting."
With a twist of his wrist, he uncorked the bottle. A faint scent drifted upward. It was remarkably clean. Cool. Not mint cool. Not medicinal either.
It reminded him of crisp winter air spilling into a warm room, carrying the sterile freshness of untouched snow.
He glanced at the bathtub. After everything the Bone-Tempering Pill had put him through, optimism no longer seemed like a survival trait.
If the elixir decided to dissolve his skin, force black sludge out of his pores, or make him vomit up half the periodic table, he would much rather it happened somewhere with a drain.
That settled it. He stepped into the empty bathtub and sat down against the sloped backrest.
"Here’s hoping you’re the friendly one."
Without giving himself time to reconsider, he tipped the bottle back.
The jade liquid slid into his mouth and he swallowed.
The elixir was the complete opposite of the pill. The pill had been fire and the elixir was cold.

Not the ordinary cold of ice or winter air. Those had limits. This cold seemed to ignore temperature altogether, slipping past his skin and settling directly into his nerves. It spread from his throat the instant he swallowed, flooding every corner of his body with a profound, unnatural chill that seemed to originate from within rather than without.
Stan shivered violently. The sensation was painful, but in an entirely different way.
The Bone-Tempering Pill had been the pain of reforging, of a foundation being broken apart and rebuilt into something stronger.
The Purity Elixir was the pain of cleansing. It felt as though every cell in his body had been seized by invisible hands and squeezed clean.
His pores opened. His organs churned. His blood seemed to surge through him with renewed purpose.
His entire body felt like a sponge saturated with years of unseen residue, now being wrung out with merciless efficiency.
A sharp gasp escaped him. Almost immediately, tiny black beads began to emerge from his skin.
They weren’t sweat. The thick, tar-like substance oozed from every pore in slow, viscous droplets, carrying with it a stench so foul that his nose instinctively recoiled.
It smelled ancient. Stale. Like something that had never been meant to remain inside a living body.
Within minutes, the water collecting beneath him had begun to darken as more of the inky residue seeped from his skin, dissolving into cloudy black ribbons before dispersing through the bath.
The pain lingered. Unlike the explosive agony of the pill, this was steady and relentless.
A deep, grinding discomfort that never quite reached unbearable heights, yet refused to lessen.
His scalp prickled incessantly. His muscles twitched. His joints throbbed with a dull ache.
His chest tightened before gradually relaxing again, as though every breath carried something unwanted out of him.
A bitter, metallic taste coated his tongue, and he found himself repeatedly spitting into the drain as his mouth continued producing foul-tasting saliva.
His eyes watered without pause. When he blinked, the tears carried faint gray streaks that vanished into the bathwater.
He endured. Compared to the Bone-Tempering Pill... This was survivable. Unpleasant, disgusting, exhausting, but survivable still...
The smell inside the bathroom steadily worsened until it bordered on unbearable. For a fleeting moment, he considered opening the window.
He dismissed the idea almost immediately. The last thing he needed was anybody catching a whiff of whatever supernatural detoxification was taking place in his apartment.
Instead, he resigned himself to the stench. The hot tap remained running, a steady stream of fresh water pouring into the tub as darkened water disappeared down the drain.
Whenever the water became too murky, he reached over, partially emptied the tub, and let it refill.
Then he settled back once more, allowing the cleansing to continue.
As before... Time quietly slipped away.
When the pain finally subsided, the bathwater had turned nearly black.
Stan slowly opened his eyes. The smell hit him immediately.

It was so overpowering he could almost taste it, a thick, nauseating stench that clung to the humid air and settled at the back of his throat. The bathtub looked like something out of a nightmare, its water dark and opaque with the impurities the elixir had forced from his body.
His skin, however... His skin felt different. He couldn’t quite explain it. It didn’t merely feel clean.
It felt... lighter and smoother.
As though an invisible layer that had always existed between his body and the world had simply disappeared.
Carefully, he sat upright. The movement was effortless.
Reaching over, he pulled the drain plug and watched the murky water swirl away into the pipes, leaving dark streaks along the porcelain before they, too, vanished beneath a stream of fresh water.
Only after the tub had emptied did he step out. He turned on the shower. Hot water cascaded over him. Once wasn’t nearly enough.
He lathered himself from head to toe, rinsed, then did it again. A third time, just to be certain.
He shampooed his hair twice, massaging his scalp until every trace of the foul residue was gone.
Using a clean washcloth, he scrubbed every inch of his body.
At first, the water running into the drain carried faint gray streaks.
Then only the slightest hint of discoloration remained.
Finally... It ran perfectly clear. Satisfied, Stan shut off the water. The sudden silence filled the bathroom.
He stepped onto the bath mat, reached into the linen closet, and wrapped himself in a fresh towel.
As he dried himself, he noticed something else. His skin wasn’t merely cleaner.
It felt unnaturally smooth beneath the towel, almost as though the texture itself had changed.
He frowned. Curiosity stirred.
With the towel draped loosely around his waist, he walked toward the bathroom mirror. He came to a stop before it. Then he looked at himself.

chapters.title: Chapter 292: The First Step: A New Beginning
paragraphs: With the towel draped loosely around his waist, Stan walked toward the bathroom mirror. He came to a stop before it. Then he looked at himself.
The man staring back at him was, quite simply, not the same man who had walked into the bathroom.
The change wasn’t dramatic. It wasn’t the sort of transformation that would make strangers stop in the street.
But to Stan, it was unmistakable.
He had lived with this face his entire life. He knew every small imperfection by memory.
They were gone.
The faint mark along his jaw had disappeared.
The slight redness across the bridge of his nose, left over from years of wearing reading glasses, had vanished.
The uneven tone on his forehead was gone.
Every minor blemish, every tiny flaw that had quietly accumulated over the years had simply ceased to exist.
His complexion possessed an almost unreal clarity. Smooth. Even. Luminous without appearing glossy.
It reminded him less of healthy skin and more of the impossibly flawless complexions found in professionally retouched magazine editorials.
His features themselves hadn’t changed. His jaw hadn’t become sharper. His cheekbones hadn’t moved. His eyes hadn’t grown larger.
Yet everything looked more defined.

Without imperfections drawing the eye away, the natural structure of his face stood out with startling clarity. His jawline appeared cleaner. His cheekbones more sculpted. Even his eyes seemed brighter, their color richer against skin that no longer carried the slightest trace of fatigue.
He had been handsome before. Objectively handsome.
The reactions he’d been receiving over the past few weeks had made that abundantly clear.
This... This was something else.
He looked impossibly refined.
The sort of appearance people spent fortunes pursuing through luxury skincare, cosmetic procedures, meticulous nutrition, and years of disciplined maintenance.
Even then, most never achieved results like this.
Some followed skincare routines that bordered on obsession. Others had access to professional makeup artists and lighting teams capable of making anyone appear flawless on camera.
Yet neither could produce skin this naturally pristine.
There was no foundation. No concealer. No carefully controlled studio lighting.
Just an ordinary bathroom mirror.
And somehow, his skin looked as though reality itself had been subtly retouched.
Stan stared at his reflection for a long moment.
"...Damn."
The quiet word escaped before he realized he’d spoken.
He slowly turned his head. The reflection mirrored the movement perfectly. He studied his profile. The clean line of his jaw. The smooth curve of his neck.
The unblemished skin across his shoulders and chest.
Even beneath the harsh white bathroom light, there wasn’t a single obvious flaw to be found.
A faint smile tugged at the corner of his mouth.
’I look ridiculous.’
Not ridiculous in the sense of being unnatural.
Ridiculous in the sense that no one had any business looking this effortlessly put together.
He gave a small, disbelieving shake of his head and stepped away from the mirror.
His eyes drifted toward the wall clock. He blinked.
Another five hours had passed.
The Purity Elixir had required five uninterrupted hours to complete its work.
Combined with the three hours consumed by the Bone-Tempering Pill, he had spent nearly eight hours undergoing two consecutive System-guided transformations.
The realization settled over him.
An entire day... gone.
Outside the bathroom window, the afternoon had given way to early evening. Warm golden light filtered through the glass, casting long shadows across the apartment.
The day was nearly over.
Stan left the bathroom and returned to his bedroom.
The stripped mattress waited where he’d left it, while the washing machine continued its steady hum somewhere down the hall.
He opened his closet and pulled out a fresh change of clothes. A soft cotton T-shirt. Dark trousers.
He dressed unhurriedly, every movement carrying the same effortless precision his body had possessed since the tempering ended.
When he finished, he stood before the full-length mirror in his bedroom.
He smoothed the front of his shirt with one hand.
Then he looked at himself again.
This time...
He wasn’t looking for what had changed.
He was trying to accept that this was simply what he looked like now.
The man reflected in the mirror was still Stan Harrison.
The same man who had woken up that morning.
The same memories.
The same ambitions.
The same quiet determination in his eyes.
And yet...
Fundamentally, he was no longer the same person.
Qi flowed through his body.
His skeleton had been tempered into something roughly five times stronger than it had been at breakfast.
His skin had been refined into a state of pristine perfection that no ordinary human should have been capable of attaining.
And somewhere in the back of his mind, the System remained quietly present, reminding him that this wasn’t the culmination of his journey.
It was the beginning.
The Bone-Tempering Pill and the Purity Elixir were merely entry-level rewards.
An introduction.
The first glimpse of what the System considered ordinary.
As the favorability of his bound targets continued to rise, stronger treasures would inevitably follow.
Stan let out a slow, measured breath.
For the first time since awakening the System, he finally possessed something he had been desperately lacking.
Context.
The ancient book had revealed the world’s forgotten history.
The pill and the elixir had proven that history beyond any possibility of doubt.
The System Shop suggested there were countless more treasures waiting to be obtained.
And his own body had become undeniable evidence that the impossible was, in fact, real.
His thoughts drifted to the final page of the book.
To the final word written there.
Antarctica.
The word lingered in his mind less like a mystery and more like a destination.
Not today.
Perhaps not tomorrow.
But someday...
He would go there.
He slipped on a light sweater over his T-shirt, picked up his phone from the bedside table, and headed toward the bedroom door.

The washing machine still hummed quietly in the laundry room. Fortunately, it was a washer-dryer, so Stan wasn’t particularly concerned despite it having run for more than five hours. He simply sighed, walked over, switched it off, and pulled out the now-clean, dry bedsheet.
Outside the windows, golden evening light had begun surrendering to dusk.
The apartment was peaceful.
Ordinary.
Yet nothing about his life was ordinary anymore.
There was still much of the evening ahead of him.
There were still people to meet. Questions to answer. Secrets to uncover.
And an entirely new path waiting to be walked.
Stan Harrison stepped out of his bedroom.
For the first time since the System had awakened, he wasn’t merely reacting to the impossible.
He was ready to begin living in it.

chapters.title: Chapter 293: A Quiet Change Of Plans
paragraphs: Stan stepped out of his apartment with loose, unhurried ease. He was hungry, but he simply wanted to eat, then spend an hour walking before the evening fully settled.
He had barely cleared the lobby when his phone buzzed in his pocket.
He pulled it out.
[Maya: I’ve sent you everything. Prospectus, financial projections, sourcing breakdown, manufacturing partner shortlist, the works. Take your time. Let me know what you think.]
He opened the files where he stood, leaning against one of the lobby’s exterior columns as he scrolled through them.
The level of detail surpassed even his expectations.

Maya had clearly been working on this for weeks, possibly months, without telling anyone. Every projection was conservative. Every assumption was carefully footnoted. Every manufacturing partner came with supporting case studies, competitive analysis, and a well-reasoned explanation for why they had made the shortlist.
By any objective standard, it was the kind of business plan a venture capitalist would describe as investment-ready.
It also became immediately obvious that Maya had no real intention of letting him invest.
The financial structure made that unmistakably clear.

She had designed the initial funding round to be covered entirely by her own capital, capital her family’s wealth easily provided. The proposed Wanhai partnership appeared only as a future revenue accelerator, not a source of funding. Every section of the plan reinforced the same philosophy: the company would be hers, built in her name, financed with her own money, while outside assistance would be limited to distribution and strategic access.
Stan let out a quiet breath and slowly shook his head.
Trying to change her mind over text would be pointless.

She hadn’t simply reached a decision, she had built an entire strategy around it. This wasn’t the kind of conversation that could happen through messages. He needed to sit across from her somewhere quiet, free of interruptions, and patiently walk her through his reasoning until she truly understood what he was trying to tell her.
He opened a new message.
[Stan: I’ve read everything. We need to talk in person. Have dinner with me tonight. There’s a quiet place near my apartment. I’ll pick you up.]
Her reply arrived less than thirty seconds later.
[Maya: Okay 😊 See you in a bit.]
Stan slipped his phone back into his pocket, abandoned the evening walk, and turned toward the parking garage.
He took the Audi and moved out. The drive to Maya’s apartment was short.

She was already waiting at the curb when he pulled up, dressed in a cream knit top and dark tailored trousers, casual, elegant, the sort of effortless outfit she wore when she wasn’t trying to make an impression. Her hair fell loose over her shoulders, and her makeup was light enough to look almost nonexistent.
She opened the passenger door, slid into the seat, and paused for the briefest moment before pulling the door shut.
Then she turned to him.
Her eyes widened, only slightly, but enough for him to notice.
"...Stan."
"Yes."
"You look..."
She trailed off, studying him. "You look different."
Stan eased the car away from the curb without looking over. "Different how?"
"I don’t know." She frowned thoughtfully, still staring. "You look like..." She tilted her head. "Did you do something to your skin? Have you been getting facials without telling me?"
"No."
"Stan." She leaned a little closer. "Your skin is glowing."
"It’s the light."
She snorted.
"It is absolutely not the light. The lighting in this car is fluorescent and deeply unflattering." She shook her head. "You look like you just walked off a magazine cover."
"I had a quiet afternoon."
"A quiet afternoon does not produce this."
She continued examining him with growing disbelief.
"You actually look... ridiculously good. Like, ridiculously good." She laughed once, almost at herself. "I’m staring, and I genuinely can’t stop. This is not a normal Tuesday evening face, Stan."
"Well, it is a normal face today."
"You’re seriously not going to tell me what you did?"
"There’s nothing to tell.
She narrowed her eyes in the familiar way she always did when she was convinced he was hiding something.
After a long moment, she sighed, leaned back into her seat, and let out a small, amused laugh.
"Fine." She folded her arms. "Be mysterious."
"I’m not mysterious."
She gave him an incredulous look. "You are extremely mysterious, Stan. You’re the definition of mysterious."
A faint smile tugged at the corner of his mouth. The conversation drifted naturally after that, but she never entirely stopped looking at him.

Every few moments, she’d steal another sideways glance, accompanied by the same faint crease between her brows, as though her mind kept circling back to the same unsolved puzzle and refusing to let it go.
The restaurant was barely ten minutes away.

She filled most of the drive with easy conversation, how the cosmetics company’s branding project was progressing, which manufacturer was beginning to edge ahead on her shortlist, and a funny story about a screenplay Sophie had insisted she read.
Stan answered easily, their conversation slipping into the comfortable rhythm that came naturally to two people who had already shared enough of themselves that there was nothing left to perform.
Still, he caught her looking at him more than once.
Each time their eyes met, a faint blush crept into her cheeks before she looked away.
He noticed every one of them. He let her look and said nothing.
The restaurant was a small, well-kept place a few blocks from his apartment, the kind of upscale neighborhood spot that served exceptional food in a quiet, warmly lit dining room.

Being popular, and having already came here with another prominent figure just this morning, the staff knew Stan well enough that the hostess greeted him with a smile before leading them to a secluded corner booth. It was the sort of booth couples gravitated toward when they wanted a conversation that belonged only to them.
Maya picked up her menu and began scanning it.
Stan opened his and turned directly to a section he had never ordered from before.

At the top of the page was the restaurant’s specialty: a slow-braised lamb shank served over saffron rice with roasted root vegetables and a rich reduction described in language that sounded as though the chef had personally written it.
He’d eaten here several times. He’d also ordered the same two or three dishes every visit. He has multiple foods he’d choose over the lamb, but tonight, he chose the lamb.

chapters.title: Chapter 294: I Told You I’d Convince You
paragraphs: Seeing Stan choose the lamb, Maya frowned in confusion as she looked up, not getting why he had done that.
"You’re not getting your favourite?"
"I felt like trying something new," he replied with a smile.
"Well it’s quite surprising for you not to order your favourite..."
"Well, I’m branching out."
She watched him with quiet amusement, as though this was yet another small detail that didn’t quite fit the version of him she’d spent the drive trying to make sense of.
"It’s good to try new things every once in a while," he said.
She tilted her head. "That’s surprisingly philosophical."
"Is it?"
"It is." She grinned. "Try new things every once in a while. That’s exactly the kind of sentence they’d print on an inspirational poster in a dentist’s waiting room."
"It’s just an observation."
She laughed. "That’s just you, isn’t it? Stan Harrison. Philosopher. Distributor of motivational poster quotes."
"Philosopher with an apparently excellent skincare routine." She then pointed at him. "Which you continue to refuse to explain."
"There’s nothing to explain, Maya."
"That," she said with satisfaction, "is exactly what someone with a secret would say."
Before he could answer, the waiter returned. Stan placed his order. The waiter turned to Maya.
She glanced at the menu for only a moment before choosing one of the least expensive dishes, a small chicken pasta.
Stan set his menu aside. "Maya."
She looked up. "Yes?"
"Order what you actually want."
"I will."
He held her gaze. "No, you’re ordering what costs the least.
She opened her mouth, then hesitated.
"You don’t want me paying for something expensive."
Silence lingered between them for a moment. Then she looked down with a sheepish smile. "...Habit."
"You never have to do that with me."
She looked back up.
Without making a production of it, he turned to the waiter.
"We’ll have two of the lamb shanks instead. And a bottle of chilled sparkling water to start. For drinks, bring us something cold that pairs well with the meal, your recommendation."
"Certainly." The waiter collected the menus and walked away.
Maya watched him for a moment before shaking her head with a quiet, affectionate smile.
"You do this every time."
"What?"
"You decide what’s best for me before I do." She laughed softly. "Then you make it happen before I’ve had the chance to argue."
"I corrected one order."
"You corrected it before I’d finished speaking."
"You were about to spend the whole meal wishing you’d ordered something else."
She narrowed her eyes playfully. "That’s a very convenient interpretation."
"It’s also the accurate one."
She laughed again, softer this time, and leaned back against the booth.
"I suppose we’ll find out."
The chilled sparkling water arrived a few moments later.
They poured themselves glasses, took a sip, and let the easy silence settle between them before the conversation turned to the reason Stan had asked her to dinner.
A gentle silence settled between them, the kind that carried the weight of unspoken things. Stan set his glass down, leaned forward slightly, and met her eyes across the table with quiet intensity.
"So," he said, his voice low and steady. "Are you really not going to let me help with the company?"
The teasing warmth of their earlier conversation evaporated. This was the moment he had brought her here for.

Maya’s gaze faltered. She tried to hold his eyes but couldn’t quite manage it. Her attention drifted to her water glass, then to the soft glow of the window, before settling somewhere near the sharp line of his jaw. A delicate flush rose along her neck and cheeks.
Stan reached across the table without hesitation.

With the gentlest touch, he caught her chin between his thumb and forefinger, turning her face toward his. The gesture was unhurried, confident, and achingly tender, the touch of a man who had learned every nuance of what she would allow, and how deeply she responded when he took exactly that much.
She let him.
"Look at me," he murmured, his voice velvet-soft. "Look at me, Maya, and refuse me to my face."
Their eyes met.

He held her there, steady and unwavering. He could feel her resolve beginning to melt beneath the weight of his gaze. Maya, with her favorability already soaring past one hundred and still climbing, was simply not built to deny him for long. Not when he looked at her like this.
But she had prepared for this.

She drew in a shaky breath and, despite the fluttering in her chest, gave him the smallest, most stubborn pout, a sweet, defiant expression that made her look impossibly young and endearing. She shook her head slowly.
"I can’t, Stan."
A slow, knowing smile curved his lips. He leaned across the table. There was only a heartbeat’s warning before his mouth found hers.
The kiss was soft, deliberate, and devastatingly romantic. His lips brushed hers with warm, unhurried pressure, tasting of the wine they’d shared and something deeper, something uniquely him.

The faint, clean scent of his skin, fresh and intoxicating, like cool mountain air and warm sunlight on clean linen, wrapped around her senses. Beneath the familiar warmth of his mouth lay a new, refreshing coolness that made her toes curl.

It was subtle, almost imperceptible, yet it sent a shiver of pure pleasure down her spine. He kissed her like he had all the time in the world to savor her, like he was committing every sigh and tremble to memory.

Maya’s thoughts scattered. She had kissed him before, but never like this. This kiss felt like a promise. Like possession wrapped in devotion. Like coming home to something she hadn’t known she was missing.
When he finally pulled back, just enough to rest his forehead lightly against hers, her eyes were dazed and her lips slightly parted.
"Okay," she whispered, before her mind had even caught up with her heart.
Stan’s smile deepened, small, warm, and utterly satisfied.
"My sweet Maya," he murmured, brushing his thumb tenderly across her flushed cheek. "I told you I’d convince you."

She drew in a shaky breath and, despite the fluttering in her chest, gave him the smallest, most stubborn pout, a sweet, defiant expression that made her look impossibly young and endearing.
She shook her head slowly.
"I can’t, Stan."
A slow, knowing smile curved his lips.
He leaned across the table.
There was only a heartbeat’s warning before his mouth found hers.
The kiss was soft, deliberate, and devastatingly romantic.
His lips brushed hers with warm, unhurried pressure, tasting of the wine they’d shared and something deeper, something uniquely him.
The faint, clean scent of his skin, fresh and intoxicating, like cool mountain air and warm sunlight on clean linen, wrapped around her senses.
Beneath the familiar warmth of his mouth lay a new, refreshing coolness that made her toes curl.
It was subtle, almost imperceptible, yet it sent a shiver of pure pleasure down her spine.
He kissed her like he had all the time in the world to savor her, like he was committing every sigh and tremble to memory.
Maya’s thoughts scattered.
She had kissed him before, but never like this.
This kiss felt like a promise.
Like possession wrapped in devotion.
Like coming home to something she hadn’t known she was missing.
When he finally pulled back, just enough to rest his forehead lightly against hers, her eyes were dazed and her lips slightly parted.
"Okay," she whispered, before her mind had even caught up with her heart.
Stan’s smile deepened, small, warm, and utterly satisfied.
"My sweet Maya," he murmured, brushing his thumb tenderly across her flushed cheek.
"I told you I’d convince you."

chapters.title: Chapter 295: Some Things Are Simply Meant To Be
paragraphs: "My sweet Maya," Stan murmured, brushing his thumb tenderly across her flushed cheek. "I told you I’d convince you."

She blinked, the lingering warmth of his mouth still tingling on hers, as the realization sank in: she had just agreed to let him invest in the company she had deliberately structured to keep him out.
Her lips formed another adorable pout. "That was a trick, Stan."
"That was negotiation," he replied, voice rich with affection.
"You kissed me into agreeing."
"You agreed," he said softly, eyes sparkling with amusement and something far deeper.
"Under duress."
"Under the most pleasant circumstances imaginable." He leaned in again, pressing a feather-light kiss to the corner of her mouth, then another to her temple. "And you liked it."

She wanted to argue. The words were already forming. But she could feel the shift inside herself, the quiet certainty that pushing further would only dim the warmth between them, and she didn’t want that. Not when being outmaneuvered by Stan felt less like defeat and more like surrendering to something inevitable and beautiful.
She let the argument go.
"Fine," she said softly, a small, rueful laugh escaping her. "But I want it structured properly. Real investment. Real equity. Real returns. Quarterly reports. Everything above board."
"Of course." His fingers traced her jaw with exquisite gentleness. "I was never going to insult you with anything less. I just needed you to accept it. Don’t worry about paying back though"
She studied him for a long moment, heart full and slightly overwhelmed.
"You’re unfair, Stan," she whispered.
"I’m fair," he countered, smiling as he tucked a strand of hair behind her ear.
"You’re unfair." Her voice was fond now, almost dreamy. "I had a whole argument prepared."
"I know. It was a very good argument."
"And you destroyed it in eight minutes."
He chuckled, low and warm, and pressed another kiss to her lips, this one slower, lingering, filled with quiet promise.
"Some things," he murmured against her mouth, "are simply meant to be."
A few minutes later, their food arrived.
The waiter set the plates down with quiet efficiency. After all she recognized that the couple in the corner booth had been in the middle of an important conversation and was now ready to eat.

The lamb shanks were generously plated, resting on saffron rice alongside roasted root vegetables. Steam curled upward, carrying the rich aromas of slow-braised meat, warm spices, and the deep, wine-dark sauce.
Stan’s expression brightened the moment his plate touched the table.
He hadn’t eaten since breakfast.

The day had wrung every ounce of energy from him. First had come three hours of the most intense pain he’d ever experienced. Then five more hours while every impurity in his body was purged at the cellular level. After that had come a long shower, clean clothes, and now dinner.
The transformation had left his body running at full tilt. His metabolism, already heightened by the system’s earlier enhancements, was demanding fuel with unmistakable urgency.
Looking at the largest dish on the menu, he found himself wondering whether it would actually be enough.
He picked up his fork. Maya watched him with quiet amusement.
"You seem really hungry."
"I am."
She smiled. "No, I mean really hungry."
"It’s been a long day."
"You skipped lunch, didn’t you?"
"I did."
"Why?"
He considered the question for a beat before answering. "Something today burned through everything I’d eaten at breakfast."
It wasn’t a lie. It just wasn’t an explanation.
She gave him a sidelong look.

It was the same look she’d worn in the car, the one that said she’d noticed another inconsistency and was quietly filing it away alongside his unusually radiant skin, his different scent, and his sudden willingness to order something new.
She let it go. For now. She picked up her own fork.
"You know," she said, "you’d make an excellent anonymous source."
"Though you going for cosmetic company is a bit confusing since you study and are more interested in acting.

"Well, if things goes well, I might discard acting entirely. Though I’m just thinking too much I’ve not even graduated yet, but you, you have the networth of an entire family as a university student how crazy is that..." She smiled.
Stan shrugged, "Well with your interrogative questions and actions I can’t tell you’d make a good journalist too, the perfect jack of all trades..."

"Well you’re right, I’ve always wanted to be a journalist since I was a kid, sadly one sometimes is forced to take a different path from their dream. But still, even though I’m no journalist, I still have their instincts and you’re going to be the death of my journalistic instincts."
Stan shrugged and she laughed, shaking her head.
"Exactly my point."
With that, they finally turned their attention to the food.
For a little while, conversation gave way to the simple pleasure of a well-earned meal.
The lamb was extraordinary.

Stan ate with the focused efficiency of a man whose body was reclaiming everything the day had taken from it. What would have been a generous portion for most people disappeared from his plate with remarkable speed.
By the time he was halfway through, Maya had stopped eating altogether.
She rested her fork against her plate and watched him. "...How are you not full yet?"
He swallowed another bite before answering. "I told you. It’s been a long day."
She glanced at what remained of his meal. "It must have been an enormous day."
"It was."
She shook her head, smiling to herself, and returned to her own dinner.
Even then, every so often, she’d glance back across the table.
There was something oddly endearing about the way he ate, direct, efficient, completely without pretense. It reminded her of how he’d played basketball: every movement purposeful, nothing wasted.
Conversation gradually wandered into lighter territory.
Maya began telling him about a Korean romance film she’d watched the night before.
"I wasn’t expecting much from it," she admitted, "and then it completely caught me off guard."

She described one scene in particular, lingering less on the dialogue than on the way it had been shot, the framing, the pacing, the silence between the characters. It was the kind of analysis only someone who lived and breathed filmmaking naturally slipped into.

chapters.title: Chapter 296: Thirty Million
paragraphs: Stan listened with genuine interest.

He found himself paying close attention not only to what she’d enjoyed, but why. The more she spoke about storytelling, the more he understood how her instincts worked. If he ever quietly helped shape another script with her, as he had with Ghost Signal, those instincts would matter.
Eventually she smiled over the rim of her glass. "So."
"What?"
"The basketball game."
"What about it?"
"Are you going to keep playing? Your team’s got another game in against a gathered up group from the science faculty."
"It’s a waste of time..."
She set her glass down. "Sophie told me this morning that the dunk clip hit Thirty million views."
He looked up from his plate. "Thirty million?"
"Yes."
"Well, that’s absurd."
"No." She laughed. "That’s reality."
She leaned forward slightly.
"There are people all over TikTuk trying to figure out where you’ve been training. Some of them are convinced you’ve been secretly working with an NBA coach."
"They’re wrong"
"They’re also trying to copy your routine."
"I don’t have a routine."
She stared at him for a beat before bursting into laughter. "That is literally the worst answer you could give the internet."
"It’s the truth."
"They’ll hate that."
"They’ll survive." He smiled.
She watched him laugh, and without meaning to, found herself smiling too.
It wasn’t even anything he’d said. She simply liked seeing him relaxed.

For a brief moment, the thought crossed Stan’s mind that her affection for him had probably deepened again over the course of the meal. The systems notification is a bit weird, it knew when to spam notification bro Stan’s view and when not to do that.
He could have checked, but he didn’t. He didn’t need to.
They ordered dessert. Maya chose the tiramisu. Stan ordered the chocolate fondant.

Both arrived a few minutes later, small, warm, and elegantly simple. At some point, without either of them commenting on it, dessert stopped being divided into hers and his. She sampled a spoonful of the fondant. He stole a bite of the tiramisu. Neither asked permission. Neither felt the need to.
It was simply what they did now. When the bill arrived, Stan reached for it.
Maya had barely begun to open her bag before he had already slipped his card into the folder.
She looked at him and he looked back. The silent exchange lasted barely a second. And then she closed her bag again.
The argument had ended before either of them had spoken.
A few minutes later, they stepped out into the cool evening air.
The streets were quieter now, the last traces of daylight giving way to the warm glow of storefronts and streetlamps.
The Audi was waiting where Stan had parked it. He walked ahead, opened the passenger door, and waited.
Maya smiled, a small, almost unconscious one, as she slid into the seat.
He closed the door gently, rounded the front of the car, and settled in behind the wheel.
The engine came to life with a low, familiar hum. For a moment, neither of them spoke. Then Maya turned her head slightly toward him.
"You taking me home?"
Stan glanced at her before easing the car away from the curb. "Of course..."
The drive back to Maya’s apartment was quiet.

Not an awkward silence, but the easy, contented kind that settled between two people after a good meal, an honest conversation, one disagreement, one kiss, and the quiet realization that everything important had been resolved.
For most of the drive, Maya leaned slightly toward him, her hand resting on the center console, close enough to his that it almost seemed absentminded.
At the second traffic light, Stan reached over and took it.
She laced her fingers through his without a word.
Neither of them felt the need to say anything. When he pulled up outside her building, Maya didn’t move to get out.
She remained where she was, her hand still in his, looking quietly through the windshield.
After a moment, she spoke. "Stan."
"Yes."
"Thank you for dinner."
"Anytime."
"And..." She smiled faintly. "Thank you for pushing me about the company."
He turned to look at her.
"I know I argued."
"Well yes you did."
"And I’m probably going to argue again tomorrow when you send me the paperwork." She teased with a smile.
"I expect you will." She laughed softly. "But... thank you."
Her thumb brushed lightly across the back of his hand.
"For caring enough not to let me push you away." His expression softened.
"Always."
She looked at him then. Really looked at him. The inexplicably clearer skin. The quiet confidence that seemed to settle naturally around him tonight. The warmth in his eyes.
Whatever had changed about him over the course of the day, she still couldn’t explain it.
She only knew she liked being near him. She leaned across the center console and kissed him.
It was slow, gentle, and unhurried.
There was no urgency in it, only affection. The kind of kiss that existed for no reason beyond wanting the other person to know exactly how much they meant.
When she finally drew back, she rested her forehead lightly against his. For a brief moment, neither of them moved.
"Goodnight, Stan."
"Goodnight."
She gave his hand one last squeeze before letting go. Then she opened the door and stepped out into the cool evening air.
Stan watched as she crossed the pavement toward the entrance.
At the door, she paused. She turned. She found him still watching.
A small smile spread across her face as she lifted a hand in a slow, unhurried wave.
He returned it. She disappeared inside. The lobby door closed behind her.
Stan remained where he was for another few seconds, the engine idling softly beneath him.
Then he eased the Audi away from the curb and pointed it toward Aurelia Heights.
The day was finally coming to an end. There was plenty waiting for him tomorrow.
The investment paperwork. The company. The system, it’s finally time to invest and see how much he’ll get from his rebate from investing in her company...
There was still those questions that still had no answers.
They could wait until morning. Tonight had been enough.
As the lights of Inksea drifted past the windshield, he found himself smiling, not broadly, just enough to feel it.
It had been an impossibly long Tuesday. Pain, transformation, business talks, dinner, and a goodnight kiss.
An entire Chapter of life compressed into a single day.
Against all reasonable expectation, he was still standing.
More than that, he was content.
And with that quiet certainty settling over him, he drove home through the glowing streets of Inksea.

chapters.title: Chapter 297: Version 2.0
paragraphs: Stan drove back to Aurelia Heights with the quiet satisfaction that always followed an evening that had unfolded exactly as he’d intended.
He had just turned onto the main avenue when a familiar system notification appeared.
[Ding!]
[Maya Zimmerman: Favorability has crossed 120.]
A faint smile tugged at the corner of his mouth.

The kiss at the restaurant had probably done it. Or perhaps their conversation about her company. Or the goodnight kiss in the car. More likely, it had been all three. Whatever combination of moments had tipped the scale, Maya had crossed the threshold cleanly. Her rebate multiplier now sat firmly in the 12× tier.
Two more notifications followed in quick succession.
[System interface update available. Tap to view.]
[Shop inventory refreshing. New items now available for purchase.]
Keeping his eyes on the road, Stan mentally opened the first notification.
The interface unfolded across his vision, cleaner and more streamlined than before. A banner at the top displayed the upgrade in crisp, understated text.
[Supreme Rebate System 2.0]
He skimmed through the upgrade summary as he drove.
The first change concerned rebate scaling.

Previously, the system had capped at a 10× multiplier once a target’s favorability exceeded 100. Now the multiplier increased progressively with higher favorability, according to a clear tiered structure:
Favorability 100-110: 10× rebate
Favorability 111-119: 11× rebate
Favorability 120-129: 12× rebate
Favorability 130-139: 13× rebate
Favorability 140+: 14× rebate and beyond, with no upper limit
Stan grasped the implications immediately.

Sophie, at 125, would now generate a 12× rebate. Maya, having just reached 120, would do the same. Amelia, who had been sitting at 128 the last time he’d checked, also qualified for the 12× tier and judging by how quickly her favorability had been climbing, she would likely break into the 13× bracket within a matter of days.
The second change increased the daily binding limit.
The original system had restricted him to two new binding per day. Version 2.0 raised that limit to four.
The implications were obvious. He could now expand his roster of bound targets four times as fast.
The third upgrade raised the weekly rebate limit for each individual target.
Instead of two rebate cycles per week, each bound target could now generate up to four.

With Sophie, Maya, Amelia, Xenia, Mia, and Sarah all maintaining exceptionally high favorability, the practical effect was staggering. Not only could he trigger rebate cycles twice as often, but the multipliers themselves were now significantly higher.
He read the summary a second time. Then he exhaled slowly. The system was no longer a curiosity.
For the first two weeks, it had been exactly that, a strange, almost amusing mechanism that quietly accumulated wealth without ever fully revealing its potential.
Version 2.0 changed that.
It wasn’t merely a convenient source of money anymore. It was infrastructure. A scalable machine. A structured engine for generating capital with extraordinary efficiency.
And with higher rebates came faster point accumulation, bringing the supernatural items in the shop within much easier reach.
The shop. The thought resurfaced.
Stan guided the Audi into his parking space at Aurelia Heights, shut off the engine, and remained seated for a moment, the interface still hovering before his eyes.
He resisted the urge to open the shop immediately.
There was something more pressing to take care of first.
He rode the elevator to his apartment, unlocked the door, tossed his keys onto the kitchen counter, and pulled out his phone.
He sat down at the dining table and opened the documents Maya had sent him.
This time, he read them with greater care.
The financial projections. The sourcing strategy. The manufacturing partner shortlist. The proposed legal structure. The brand positioning. The five-year expansion plan.

He worked through every page with the focused concentration of a man preparing to commit a meaningful portion of his liquid capital. Before making that decision, he wanted to understand exactly what he was funding.
The plan was solid. Not merely optimistic, professionally viable.

Given competent execution and the right partnerships, Maya’s company could realistically begin generating meaningful revenue within eighteen months and establish itself as a respectable mid-tier cosmetics manufacturer within three years.

The Wanhai partnership, the one Stan would now arrange quietly through his own connections instead of relying on Wanhai’s public supplier network, would likely shorten that timeline by at least a year.
Even if the proposal hadn’t been this strong, he would have invested anyway.
The system’s rebate mechanics made the decision difficult to ignore.
Maya’s favorability had just crossed 120, placing her firmly in the 12× rebate tier. Every dollar he invested in her company would ultimately return to him twelvefold.
But the fact that the business itself was genuinely promising made the decision far cleaner.
He wasn’t bankrolling a vanity project or rescuing a failing startup.
He was investing in a company with a credible business model, realistic projections, and the potential to create substantial long-term value.
The rebate wasn’t the reason the investment made sense.
It was simply an extraordinary bonus attached to an already sound opportunity.
Stan opened his banking app. His available liquid balance stood at approximately $620 million.

That morning’s billion-dollar conversion into a single system point had carved a noticeable chunk out of his holdings, but what remained was still more money than most people would see in several lifetimes.

According to Maya’s projections, the company required an initial investment of $8 million to $12 million. That would cover the manufacturing facility lease, the first round of equipment purchases, eighteen months of payroll, initial inventory, and a healthy working capital reserve.
Eight to twelve million dollars. Stan studied the figure in silence. Then he made his decision.
He wasn’t going to invest eight to twelve million dollars in Maya’s company.
He was going to invest all of it. The full $620 million. By any rational standard, the amount was absurd.

Maya didn’t need that much capital. Her company couldn’t deploy it efficiently in its first year, or even its second. The investment exceeded the business’s projected capital requirements by well over fifty times.
But Stan wasn’t optimizing for Maya’s balance sheet. He was optimizing for the rebate.
Ever since the system had awakened, he’d barely scratched the surface of what it could do.

His first few bindings had produced extraordinary returns, Sophie’s $1.4 billion, Amelia’s $300 million, yet over the past two weeks he had done very little to create additional rebate cycles. His personal spending was negligible compared to his wealth. His investments had been conservative. The system had quietly waited for him to use it as intended.
He hadn’t. That changed tonight. Earlier that afternoon, he had spent $1 billion on a single book. The price had been one system point. The implication was unsettling.

That book had been nothing more than an introductory text. If future shop items included genuine cultivation manuals, advanced pills, artifacts, weapons, intelligence assets, or other supernatural resources, their prices would almost certainly be measured in multiple system points.
At the current exchange rate, each point represented a billion dollars.
Which meant he would eventually need billions, perhaps tens of billions, in liquid capital simply to keep pace with what the shop offered.
He could no longer think in terms of millions. The scale had changed.
If the system demanded billions, then he needed an engine capable of producing billions.
Tonight would be the beginning. With that, Stan opened his banking app.

He had just turned onto the main avenue when a familiar system notification appeared.
[Ding!]
[Maya Zimmerman: Favorability has crossed 120.]
A faint smile tugged at the corner of his mouth.
The kiss at the restaurant had probably done it.
Or perhaps their conversation about her company.
Or the goodnight kiss in the car.
More likely, it had been all three.
Whatever combination of moments had tipped the scale, Maya had crossed the threshold cleanly.
Her rebate multiplier now sat firmly in the 12× tier.
Two more notifications followed in quick succession.
[System interface update available.
Tap to view.]
[Shop inventory refreshing.
New items now available for purchase.]
Keeping his eyes on the road, Stan mentally opened the first notification.
The interface unfolded across his vision, cleaner and more streamlined than before.
A banner at the top displayed the upgrade in crisp, understated text.
[Supreme Rebate System 2.0]
He skimmed through the upgrade summary as he drove.
The first change concerned rebate scaling.
Previously, the system had capped at a 10× multiplier once a target’s favorability exceeded 100.
Now the multiplier increased progressively with higher favorability, according to a clear tiered structure:
Favorability 100-110: 10× rebate
Favorability 111-119: 11× rebate
Favorability 120-129: 12× rebate
Favorability 130-139: 13× rebate
Favorability 140+: 14× rebate and beyond, with no upper limit
Stan grasped the implications immediately.
Sophie, at 125, would now generate a 12× rebate.
Maya, having just reached 120, would do the same.

Amelia, who had been sitting at 128 the last time he’d checked, also qualified for the 12× tier and judging by how quickly her favorability had been climbing, she would likely break into the 13× bracket within a matter of days.
The second change increased the daily binding limit.
The original system had restricted him to two new binding per day.
Version 2.0 raised that limit to four.
The implications were obvious.
He could now expand his roster of bound targets four times as fast.
The third upgrade raised the weekly rebate limit for each individual target.
Instead of two rebate cycles per week, each bound target could now generate up to four.
With Sophie, Maya, Amelia, Xenia, Mia, and Sarah all maintaining exceptionally high favorability, the practical effect was staggering.
Not only could he trigger rebate cycles twice as often, but the multipliers themselves were now significantly higher.

A scalable machine.
A structured engine for generating capital with extraordinary efficiency.

The sourcing strategy.
The manufacturing partner shortlist.
The proposed legal structure.
The brand positioning.
The five-year expansion plan.

Before making that decision, he wanted to understand exactly what he was funding.
The plan was solid.
Not merely optimistic, professionally viable.
